tamil:
அகர முதல எழுத்தெல்லாம் ஆதி
பகவன் முதற்றே உலகு.
transliteration:
Agara mudhala ezhuthu ellaam aadhi,
Pakavan mudhatre ulagu.
current_meaning: Just as the letter “A” stands first among all the letters of the alphabet, God stands first as the origin and foundation of the whole world.
elementary_explanation: The alphabet always starts with the letter A, and everything else is built from it. This kural says God is like that letter A for the whole world — the very first thing, the starting point everything else comes from.
university_explanation: Valluvar opens his work not with an invocation to a specific deity but with a logical analogy drawn from language itself: just as அ (a) is structurally primary in the Tamil alphabet — the vowel from which the entire phonetic system is generated — so too is “Pahavan” (rendered here “God”/“the Primal Being”) ontologically primary to the cosmos. The term is deliberately non-sectarian, part of why the Thirukkural has been embraced across Saiva, Vaishnava, Jain, and secular-humanist readings alike. The appeal to a “first principle” or arche is one of the oldest moves in both theology and philosophy — found equally in Vedic cosmology, biblical self-declaration, and Aristotelian metaphysics.

tamil:
கற்றதனால் ஆய பயனென்கொல் வாலறிவன்
நற்றாள் தொழாஅர் எனின்.
transliteration:
Katradhanaal aaya payan en kol vaal-arivan,
natraal thozhaaar enin.
current_meaning: What good is all of a person’s learning, if they never bow in reverence to the good feet of the One of pure, perfect wisdom?
elementary_explanation: Imagine acing every test but never once saying thank you to your teacher. This kural says learning without being humble and thankful toward God doesn’t really count for much.
university_explanation: This verse critiques a purely instrumental or accumulative view of education. “Vaal-arivan” (“the one of spotless/pure knowledge”) refers to a transcendent, perfect intelligence — the ground of all true knowing, not a sectarian god. Valluvar’s claim is that erudition divorced from reverence toward that ultimate source is functionally sterile: it produces information without transformation. This is a recurring cross-cultural theme — the distinction between accumulated data and lived, humbling wisdom.

tamil:
மலர்மிசை ஏகினான் மாணடி சேர்ந்தார்
நிலமிசை நீடுவாழ் வார்.
transliteration:
Malar-misai Ekinaan maanadi serndhaar,
nila-misai needu vaazhvaar.
current_meaning: Those who cling to the glorious feet of Him who moves lightly even upon a flower will live long and flourish upon this earth.
elementary_explanation: Picture someone so light and gentle they could stand on a flower without crushing it. This kural says if you hold on tight to someone that good — meaning you stay close to God — your life goes well for a long time.
university_explanation: The image of the divine “moving upon a flower” evokes both lightness/purity and the lotus-throne motif common to Tamil and broader Indic religious iconography. “Nilamisai needuvaazhvaar” — “shall live long upon the earth” — is classically read not as mere biological longevity but as a durable, well-founded flourishing that outlasts the transient. The pairing of devotion with durable flourishing is one of the most cross-culturally attested religious claims.

tamil:
வேண்டுதல் வேண்டாமை இலானடி சேர்ந்தார்க்கு
யாண்டும் இடும்பை இல.
transliteration:
Vendudhal vendaamai ilaan adi serndhaarkku,
yaandum idumbai ila.
current_meaning: No suffering will ever touch those who take refuge in the feet of the One who is beyond all craving and all aversion.
elementary_explanation: Some people get super excited when they get what they want, and really upset when they don’t. This kural says if you can stay as calm as God — not too excited, not too upset — bad things can’t really shake you.
university_explanation: The verse names two categories — raga (craving/attachment) and dvesha (aversion) — as the very things the Divine transcends. This dyad is the central diagnostic pair in most Indian soteriologies for why beings suffer. The claim is that participation in a consciousness beyond craving/aversion is itself what removes vulnerability to affliction — functionally identical to the Stoic and Buddhist claims that suffering arises from the mind’s reactive patterns rather than external events themselves.

tamil:
இருள்சேர் இருவினையும் சேரா இறைவன்
பொருள்சேர் புகழ்புரிந்தார் மாட்டு.
transliteration:
Irul-ser iru-vinaiyum seraa iraivan,
porul-ser pukazh-purindhaar maattu.
current_meaning: The two dark deeds — the good and bad karma born of ignorance — will not attach themselves to those who truly delight in praising God with real understanding.
elementary_explanation: Imagine collecting points for good things and bad things you do, without really understanding why they matter. This kural says truly understanding and loving God wipes the whole scoreboard clean — good points and bad.
university_explanation: “Irul” (darkness) signifies avidya (ignorance), and “iru vinai” (the twin deeds) refers to punya and papa — meritorious and demeritorious karma — both of which bind the soul to rebirth regardless of whether the deeds were “good” or “bad,” because both are performed from a standpoint of ignorance. Valluvar’s claim is that liberation is not more good karma outweighing bad, but a shift in understanding that removes a person from the karmic ledger altogether.

tamil:
பொறிவாயில் யைந்தவித்தான் பொய்தீர் ஒழுக்க
நெறிநின்றார் நீடுவாழ் வார்.
transliteration:
Pori-vaayil aindhu avithaan poi-theer ozhukka,
neri ninRaar needu vaazhvaar.
current_meaning: Those who stand firm in the untainted, truthful path of Him who has mastered the five sense-desires will live long, flourishing lives.
elementary_explanation: We have five senses — seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching — and they can pull us all over the place wanting things. This kural says if you master your five senses instead of letting them boss you around, your life goes really well.
university_explanation: “Pori” refers to the five sense-faculties (indriyas); the divine is depicted as the paradigm of complete indriya-nigraha (sense-mastery), a central discipline across nearly all Indian contemplative systems. The verse makes mastery of the senses, rather than mere rule-following, the actual mechanism of a flourishing life — free from the erratic disturbance the unchecked senses cause.

tamil:
தனக்குவமை இல்லாதான் தாள்சேர்ந்தார்க் கல்லால்
மனக்கவலை மாற்றல் அரிது.
transliteration:
Thanakku-uvamai illaadhaan thaal serndhaark kallaal,
mana-kavalai maatral aridhu.
current_meaning: Except for those who cling to the feet of the One beyond all comparison, it is very hard for anyone to be free of the mind’s anxieties.
elementary_explanation: Everybody worries sometimes. This kural says the only way to truly stop worrying deep down is to hold onto something so great that nothing else can compare to it.
university_explanation: “Thanakku uvamai illaadhaan” (“the One with no likeness to Himself”) situates the removal of mental anxiety not in technique or willpower but in relationship to a reality that relativizes every other object of comparison. If nothing else is truly comparable, ordinary anxieties (always about something comparable — status, loss, gain) lose their grip. This mirrors a recurring move across theistic and philosophical traditions: relocating the anxious self’s center of gravity onto something that cannot be lost or reduced by comparison.

tamil:
அறவாழி அந்தணன் தாள்சேர்ந்தார்க் கல்லால்
பிறவாழி நீந்தல் அரிது.
transliteration:
Aravaazhi andhanan thaal serndhaark kallaal,
piRa vaazhi neendhal aridhu.
current_meaning: Except for those who cling to the feet of the gracious One who is like an ocean of virtue, it is hard for anyone to swim across the other ocean — the ocean of worldly existence.
elementary_explanation: Picture two huge oceans: one is how good God is, and the other is all of life’s ups and downs. This kural says the only way to cross the hard ocean is to hold onto the good one.
university_explanation: “Aravaazhi” (“ocean of dharma/virtue”) figures the divine as boundless moral reality, an ocean whose scale matches the second ocean it lets one cross — “piravaazhi,” the vast ocean of worldly existence one must traverse. The parallel construction is a deliberate rhetorical mirroring, reinforcing that only something of equal or greater vastness than the ocean of worldly existence can carry a being across it.

tamil:
கோளில் பொறியின் குணமிலவே எண்குணத்தான்
தாளை வணங்காத் தலை.
transliteration:
Kolil poRiyin guNam-ilavey,
eN-guNaththaan thaalai vaNangaadha thalai.
current_meaning: A head that will not bow to the feet of the One possessed of the eight great virtues is as useless as a sense-organ that has lost its power to sense.
elementary_explanation: Think of an eye that can’t see, or an ear that can’t hear — totally useless, right? This kural says a person who won’t bow to God is just as useless, no matter how proud or important they feel.
university_explanation: “Eṇ-guṇam” (“the eight qualities”) refers to a catalogue of divine perfections in Tamil Saiva/Vaishnava theology. The verse’s force lies in its analogy: a sense organ that has lost its functional capacity is not merely deficient but categorically useless — it fails at the one thing that defines it. Likewise, a head that will not bow is said to fail at the one thing Valluvar treats as most defining meaningful personhood: right relationship, through humility, to the ultimate reality.

tamil:
பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல் நீந்துவர் நீந்தார்
இறைவன் அடிசேரா தார்.
transliteration:
PiRavi-p perungadal neendhuvar neendhaar,
iRaivan adi seraadhaar.
current_meaning: Only those who reach the feet of God can swim across the great ocean of repeated births; no one else can.
elementary_explanation: Life — with all its ups, downs, and being born again and again — is like a giant ocean. This last kural in the chapter says the only way to swim all the way across it is by holding onto God.
university_explanation: This closing verse restates and intensifies kural 8’s ocean imagery, now naming the object to be crossed explicitly as “piravi” — birth/rebirth itself — invoking the doctrine of samsara common to the Indian religious milieu. The repetition is a structural device: the chapter opens by establishing God as “first” of all things and closes by establishing God as the only viable “crossing” out of the cycle those origins set in motion.

tamil:
வான்நின்று உலகம் வழங்கி வருதலால்
தான்அமிழ்தம் என்றுணரற் பாற்று.
transliteration:
Vaan nindru ulagam vazhangi varudhalaal,
Thaan amizhdham endru unarar paatru.
current_meaning: Because the world keeps going and living only through rain that falls without fail, rain itself deserves to be recognised as amrita — the nectar that sustains undying life.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a plant on your windowsill. Water it, and it stays green and grows; forget it for a week, and it droops and dies. This kural says the whole world is that plant, and rain is the water. Because rain keeps everything alive, we should treat it like the most precious drink there is.
university_explanation: Valluvar's second chapter makes a striking structural choice: immediately after invoking God he turns not to ritual or scripture but to வான் (vaan), the sky and the rain that comes from it. The key term is அமிழ்தம் (amizhdham), the Tamil form of Sanskrit अमृत (amṛta), the deathless nectar of the gods — so rain is not merely useful but the very substance of continued life, which is why G. U. Pope rendered it "the true ambrosial food of all that lives." The verb வழங்கி (vazhangi, "conducting itself, carrying on") frames the world as an ongoing transaction that rain alone keeps in motion. Medieval commentators such as Parimelazhagar read the chapter as establishing the material precondition of அறம் (aram, virtue) itself, and modern secular and ecological readers have seized on exactly this move: Valluvar grounds ethics in a physical dependency rather than in divine command.

tamil:
துப்பார்க்குத் துப்பாய துப்பாக்கித் துப்பார்க்குத்
துப்பாய தூஉம் மழை.
transliteration:
Thuppaarkkuth thuppaaya thuppaakkith thuppaarkkuth,
Thuppaaya thooum mazhai.
current_meaning: Rain produces the food that those who eat will eat, and then, for those same eaters, rain becomes the drink they drink; it is both the maker of food and food itself.
elementary_explanation: Rain is like a cook who grows the vegetables, cooks the meal, and then also pours you a glass of water to go with it. It does both jobs at once — it makes your food, and it is your drink.
university_explanation: This is one of the most technically dazzling couplets in the Kural: the syllable துப்பு (thuppu) is repeated five times, shifting sense each time between "food/sustenance," "strength," and the verbal sense "to eat or enjoy," a figure Tamil poetics calls யமகம் (yamakam). The elongated தூஉம் (thooum) is an அளபெடை, a metrical lengthening that also lets the word carry the sense of drinking. Semantically the verse makes a double claim that anticipates modern hydrology and nutrition alike — rain is the upstream cause of food and is simultaneously the substance consumed — a point later elaborated in chapter 104 on உழவு (agriculture). Commentators from Parimelazhagar to Salomon Pappaiah note that this two-sidedness is precisely why rain, and not the farmer, is given primacy in the book's opening argument.

tamil:
விண்இன்று பொய்ப்பின் விரிநீர் வியனுலகத்து
உள்நின்று உடற்றும் பசி.
transliteration:
Vin indru poyppin virineer viyanulagaththu,
Ul nindru udatrum pasi.
current_meaning: If the sky breaks its promise and no rain comes, then hunger will take up residence inside this wide, sea-encircled world and torment every life in it.
elementary_explanation: Imagine standing right next to a swimming pool while you are terribly thirsty — all that water, and not a drop you can drink. This kural says the world is surrounded by ocean, but if rain stops falling, people will still go hungry, and hunger will hurt from the inside.
university_explanation: The verb பொய்ப்பின் (poyppin) literally means "if it lies" — Valluvar personifies the sky as a party that can break faith, which is why English renderings often speak of clouds that "deceive." The phrase விரிநீர் வியனுலகம் (virineer viyanulagam), "the broad world of spreading waters," sets up a deliberate irony: a planet ringed by ocean can still starve, because salt sea is not rain. உடற்றும் (udatrum) is a strong verb of tormenting or harrying, and உள்நின்று (ul nindru, "standing within") places the affliction inside the body rather than outside it. The couplet is frequently cited in modern Tamil discussion of drought and food security precisely because it distinguishes water-in-general from usable fresh water.

tamil:
ஏரின் உழாஅர் உழவர் புயல்என்னும்
வாரி வளங்குன்றிக் கால்.
transliteration:
Erin uzhaaar uzhavar puyal ennum,
Vaari valam kundrik kaal.
current_meaning: When rain — that great revenue-stream — falls short in its yield, even the farmers will stop driving the plough.
elementary_explanation: A bicycle is useless if the tyres have no air in them; you can own it, but you cannot ride it. This kural says a farmer's plough is like that. However strong the farmer is, if the rain does not come, the plough just sits there.
university_explanation: The economic vocabulary here is deliberate: வாரி (vaari) is a revenue term, the yield or income of a realm, so Valluvar literally calls rain the kingdom's principal income stream — a framing that anticipates the Poruṭpāl's treatment of statecraft and chapter 104 on உழவு (agriculture). உழாஅர் (uzhaaar, "they do not plough") carries an அளபெடை, a metrical elongation that lends the line a note of weary finality. புயல் (puyal) denotes rain in its abundant, gusting monsoon form rather than a drizzle. The couplet's force lies in its choice of the farmer as subject: of all people the ploughman is the most industrious, and if even he downs tools, no amount of human effort can substitute for the sky.

tamil:
கெடுப்பதூஉம் கெட்டார்க்குச் சார்வாய்மற் றாங்கே
எடுப்பதூஉம் எல்லாம் மழை.
transliteration:
Keduppadhoum kettaarkkuch chaarvaai matraange,
Eduppadhoum ellaam mazhai.
current_meaning: Rain is what ruins people, and rain is also what comes alongside the ruined and raises them up again — it does both, and it does all of it.
elementary_explanation: Fire can burn your hand, and fire can also cook your dinner — the same thing can hurt you or help you. This kural says rain is like that: too little or too much can wreck everything, and then the right rain at the right time puts it all back together.
university_explanation: The couplet is built on a tight antithesis — கெடுப்பது ("that which destroys") against எடுப்பது ("that which lifts up") — each carrying the அளபெடை elongation -தூஉம் that gives the line its rocking, pendulum rhythm. Commentators divide on the mechanism of ruin: Parimelazhagar reads கெடுப்பது as rain destroying by withholding itself, while modern paraphrasts such as Kalaignar Karunanidhi allow the destructive flood as well, and both readings are defensible from the Tamil. Strikingly, Valluvar assigns the double agency to rain itself rather than to a god who sends it, and the closing எல்லாம் ("all of it") refuses to split the credit. The verse is a favourite of Tamil ecological writing because it treats the same natural force as both hazard and remedy without moralising either face.

tamil:
விசும்பின் துளிவீழின் அல்லால்மற் றாங்கே
பசும்புல் தலைகாண்பு அரிது.
transliteration:
Visumbin thulivizhin allaal matraange,
Pasumpul thalaikaanbu aridhu.
current_meaning: Unless drops fall from the open sky, it will be hard to catch sight of even the tip of a single blade of green grass on the earth.
elementary_explanation: Put a seed in a pot of soil and give it no water at all. Nothing happens — not even a tiny green shoot. This kural says that is what the whole world would look like without rain: not one blade of grass anywhere.
university_explanation: விசும்பு (visumbu) is the open expanse of sky rather than the cloud, so the drop is imagined falling from the whole heavens at once. The argument is a fortiori and depends on Tamil biological classification: பசும்புல் (pasumpul), green grass, is the standard example of an ஓரறிவு உயிர் — a one-sense living being, the humblest grade of life in the Tamil-Jain scheme — so if even that cannot appear, nothing above it can. தலை here means the tip or head of the blade, sharpening the claim from "no grass" to "not even the tip of grass." The verse's spare, almost photographic minimalism has made it one of the most quoted lines of the chapter in Tamil environmental writing.

tamil:
நெடுங்கடலும் தன்நீர்மை குன்றும் தடிந்தெழிலி
தான்நல்கா தாகி விடின்.
transliteration:
Nedungadalum than neermai kundrum thadinthezhili,
Thaan nalkaadhaagi vidin.
current_meaning: Even the long, vast sea will diminish in its own fullness if the cloud that has drawn its water up stops giving that water back.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a piggy bank you keep taking coins out of but never put any coins back into. Sooner or later it is empty. This kural says even the huge ocean is like that piggy bank: the clouds take water from it, and if they never return it as rain, even the sea runs low.
university_explanation: எழிலி (ezhili) is the rain-cloud and தடிந்து means "having cut off, drawn up," so the line describes evaporation as an act of extraction from the sea. The phrase தன் நீர்மை (than neermai) is a fine pun: நீர்மை means both "wateriness, fullness of water" and "one's own proper nature or quality," so the sea loses its water and its character at once. What makes the couplet remarkable is that it states a closed evaporation-and-precipitation cycle — cloud takes from ocean, must return to ocean — many centuries before that cycle was formalised in European science. Commentators from Parimelazhagar onward also read a social allegory here, developed vigorously by Kalaignar Karunanidhi: those who rise out of a community and do not give back diminish the very source that raised them.

tamil:
சிறப்பொடு பூசனை செல்லாது வானம்
வறக்குமேல் வானோர்க்கும் ஈண்டு.
transliteration:
Sirappodu poosanai sellaadhu vaanam,
Varakkumel vaanorkkum eendu.
current_meaning: If the sky dries up, then here on earth neither the great festivals nor the daily worship offered to the celestials can go on at all.
elementary_explanation: You cannot have a birthday party if there is no food, no cake and no candles — the party just does not happen. This kural says the same about temple festivals and daily prayers: if the rain stops, there is nothing left to offer, and the celebrating stops too.
university_explanation: பூசனை (poosanai), from Sanskrit पूजा, denotes the regular daily offering, while சிறப்பு (sirappu) here carries its technical sense of the annual festival or special honour, so the couplet covers the whole ritual calendar from daily to yearly. வானோர் (vaanor), "those of the sky," is a neat counterpoint to வானம், the sky itself — the sky-dwellers are made hostage to the sky's own generosity. The adverb ஈண்டு ("here," i.e. in this world) localises the collapse: heaven is not harmed, but heaven's honours on earth cease. The argument is quietly subversive of ritual priority, inverting the ordinary Vedic sequence in which sacrifice causes rain, and it is one of the passages most often cited to show Valluvar's materially grounded, non-sectarian ethics.

tamil:
தானம் தவம்இரண்டும் தங்கா வியன்உலகம்
வானம் வழங்கா தெனின்.
transliteration:
Thaanam thavam irandum thangaa viyan ulagam,
Vaanam vazhangaadhenin.
current_meaning: If the sky stops giving its rain, then neither charity toward others nor austerity practised on one's own account can survive anywhere in this wide world.
elementary_explanation: You cannot share your lunch with a friend if you have no lunch, and it is not brave to skip a meal if there was never any food to skip. This kural says that giving to others and going without on purpose both need there to be something in the world first — and rain is what puts it there.
university_explanation: The two nouns are the twin pillars of Valluvar's ethical architecture: தானம் (thaanam, Sanskrit dāna) is the householder's virtue of giving, treated at length in chapter 23 ஈகை, while தவம் (thavam, Sanskrit tapas) is the renunciant's discipline, treated in chapter 27. By yoking them in a single line and making both contingent on rainfall, Valluvar establishes the material precondition of the entire இல்லறவியல் and துறவறவியல் sections before he has begun to expound either. The verb தங்கா ("will not abide, will not stay") is carefully chosen — it is not that such acts become wrong, but that they can no longer hold their place in the world. The move is characteristic: ethics in the Kural is never floated free of the economy that supports it.

tamil:
நீர்இன்று அமையாது உலகெனின் யார்யார்க்கும்
வான்இன்று அமையாது ஒழுக்கு.
transliteration:
Neer indru amaiyaadhu ulagenin yaaryaarkkum,
Vaan indru amaiyaadhu ozhukku.
current_meaning: If it is true that the world cannot carry on for anyone at all without water, then it is just as true that right conduct cannot carry on without rain.
elementary_explanation: Think of electricity in a house. The lights, the fridge, the heating — none of it works if the power is cut. This kural says rain is the power supply for the whole world, and even being good to each other gets much harder when it fails.
university_explanation: The couplet's force rests on a deliberate pun in its final word, ஒழுக்கு (ozhukku), which means both "a flowing, a stream" and, through its near-twin ஒழுக்கம், "right conduct" — the subject of chapter 14. Valluvar thereby makes one word carry both the hydrological and the moral sense of "keeping to its proper course," closing the chapter by fusing the two. யார்யார்க்கும் ("for anyone whosoever") universalises the claim across rank, region and creed, an emphasis that recurs throughout the Kural's ethics. Placed as the last verse of the chapter, it is the hinge that carries the reader into chapters 3 and 4 on the greatness of the renunciant and the assertion of virtue: the whole moral edifice that follows has just been shown to rest on rainfall.

tamil:
ஒழுக்கத்து நீத்தார் பெருமை விழுப்பத்து
வேண்டும் பனுவல் துணிவு.
transliteration:
Ozhukkaththu neeththaar perumai vizhuppaththu,
Vendum panuval thunivu.
current_meaning: The settled conclusion of every worthwhile book is that the greatness of those who, standing firm in their own discipline, have let go of desire should be praised above all other excellence.
elementary_explanation: Imagine every good book in the world lined up on one shelf, and you ask them all the same question: “Who is the greatest kind of person?” This kural says they would all give the same answer — the person who keeps to good habits and stops grabbing for things they want.
university_explanation: Valluvar grounds the authority of asceticism not in revelation but in textual consensus: “panuval thunivu” means literally “the settled resolution (thunivu) of learned works (panuval).” His renunciant is “neeththaar,” “those who have let go” — a participle from nee- (to leave, to separate) rather than a sectarian title such as sannyāsin or bhikkhu, so the ascetic is defined by an act rather than by membership in an order. Crucially he binds renunciation to “ozhukkam,” disciplined conduct, refusing to let letting-go collapse into licence: greatness belongs only to those who stand “ozhukkaththu,” inside conduct. The word “vizhuppam” (pre-eminence, the choicest thing) makes the claim comparative rather than merely approving — not that renunciation is good, but that it is the highest good the books know. This opening move is characteristic of Tamil didactic poetry, which establishes authority by appeal to accumulated learned opinion, and it lets the chapter exalt renunciants without endorsing any one religion's account of why they matter.

tamil:
துறந்தார் பெருமை துணைக்கூறின் வையத்து
இறந்தாரை எண்ணிக்கொண் டற்று.
transliteration:
Thurandhaar perumai thunaikkoorin vaiyaththu,
Irandhaarai ennikkon datru.
current_meaning: To try to state how great those who have renounced are is like trying to count every person who has ever died on this earth.
elementary_explanation: Imagine someone asked you to count every leaf that has ever fallen from every tree in the world. You could start, but you could never finish. This kural says that asking “how great are people who have let go of wanting things?” is that same kind of question — too big to ever finish counting.
university_explanation: The force of the verse is in “thunaik-koorin” — “if one were to say the measure (thunai) of it.” Thunai here is quantity, extent, an amount; the couplet is not saying the renunciant's greatness is hard to describe but that it is the wrong sort of thing to put a number on. The chosen comparison is deliberately brutal: “vaiyaththu irandhaarai ennikkondu,” tallying up everyone who has ever died in the world, an arithmetic that is not merely large but principled endless, since the dead accumulate faster than any count. Commentators from Parimelazhagar onward read the simile as one of category error rather than mere magnitude. Placed second in the chapter, it functions as a rhetorical guard-rail: having just claimed in Kural 21 that the books rank renunciants highest, Valluvar immediately blocks the reader from imagining that this ranking could be cashed out in any scale or quantity.

tamil:
இருமை வகைதெரிந்து ஈண்டுஅறம் பூண்டார்
பெருமை பிறங்கிற்று உலகு.
transliteration:
Irumai vakaitherindhu eendaram poondaar,
Perumai pirangitru ulagu.
current_meaning: Nothing shines higher in this world than the greatness of those who, having discerned the two orders of existence, have taken up the life of virtue here and now.
elementary_explanation: Some people look at two roads and can actually tell which one leads somewhere good and which one just looks fun for a little while. This kural says the people who can tell the difference — and then actually start walking the good road today, not someday — are the brightest people in the whole world.
university_explanation: “Irumai” — “twoness” — is the pivot, and the commentators do not agree on what the two are. Parimelazhagar takes them as this birth and the next (iham and param); Manakkudavar and several modern readers take them as birth and release from birth, the round of rebirth against liberation; a third reading makes them pleasure and good, the transient and the abiding. Valluvar leaves the ambiguity intact, which is characteristic: what matters is not which pair you name but that you have actually distinguished (“vakai therindhu,” sorted out the kinds) rather than drifted. Against that discernment he sets the sharply temporal “eendu” — here, in this place, in this life — so that the verse refuses to let the insight be postponed to a future existence. “Pirangitru” (from pirangu-, to shine forth, to be conspicuous) makes the resulting greatness visible in the world rather than hidden in it; the renunciant's virtue is not an inward secret but the brightest public fact the world contains.

tamil:
உரனென்னும் தோட்டியான் ஓரைந்தும் காப்பான்
வரனென்னும் வைப்பிற்கோர் வித்து.
transliteration:
Uranennum thottiyaan oraindhum kaappaan,
Varanennum vaippirkor viththu.
current_meaning: The one who holds all five senses in check with the goad called firmness of mind is a seed for that highest of all estates, liberation.
elementary_explanation: A person riding a huge elephant carries a small hooked stick, and with that one little stick they can steer an animal far stronger than they are. This kural says your five senses are like five elephants, and a steady mind is the little hook that steers them — and steering them is how something wonderful gets planted.
university_explanation: The image is precise and technical: “thotti” is the ankusa, the mahout's hooked goad, and the “oraindhu,” the five, are the sense-faculties imagined as five rutting elephants. Against their bulk Valluvar sets “uran,” mental firmness or resolve — the smallest instrument mastering the largest force, which is the whole argument of the verse in one picture. The payoff clause is theologically loaded: “varan” (from Sanskrit vara, the choicest) names the supreme estate, and “vaippu” is a deposit or treasure-store, so the ascetic becomes “or viththu,” a single seed, for that store. The seed metaphor matters — the sense-controller is not said to have arrived, but to be the germ from which the highest state grows, which keeps the emphasis on practice rather than attainment. The Tamil Shaiva tradition heard this verse as close kin to Tirumular's Tirumandiram, which likewise sets the goad of knowledge against the elephants of the senses.

tamil:
ஐந்தவித்தான் ஆற்றல் அகல்விசும்பு ளார்கோமான்
இந்திரனே சாலுங் கரி.
transliteration:
Aindhaviththaan aatral akalvisumbu ulaarkoman,
Indhirane saalung kari.
current_meaning: Indra himself, lord of the dwellers in the wide heavens, is proof enough of the power of the one who has extinguished the desires of all five senses.
elementary_explanation: Imagine the strongest king in the world admitting that someone else is stronger than him. That would settle the argument, wouldn't it? This kural says the king of the sky-world himself is the living proof of how powerful a person becomes when they put out the fire of wanting.
university_explanation: “Aindhavith-thaan” is built on avi-, to extinguish or quench, so the ascetic has not merely restrained the five but put them out, as one puts out a lamp. Against this Valluvar sets a legal metaphor: Indra, “akal visumbu ulaar koman,” king of those in the wide sky, is the “kari” — the witness, the one whose testimony settles a case. The choice of Indra is doubly pointed. In Puranic narrative Indra's own sovereignty was won by tapas, so his throne is itself an exhibit of what austerity produces; and Indra is famously the god who panics when a human ascetic's penance grows strong enough to threaten his seat, which makes his testimony that of a reluctant expert witness. Some commentators, including Parimelazhagar, also read a darker allusion to the Ahalya episode, in which Indra's own failure to quench desire cost him everything — in which case the god testifies not by his glory but by his fall. Notably, the Kural cites Indra only as evidence, never as an object of worship.

tamil:
செயற்கரிய செய்வார் பெரியர் சிறியர்
செயற்கரிய செய்கலா தார்.
transliteration:
Seyarkariya seyvaar periyar siriyar,
Seyarkariya seykalaa thaar.
current_meaning: The great are those who do what is hard to do; the small are those who cannot do what is hard to do.
elementary_explanation: Two people stand in front of the same steep hill. One starts climbing even though it hurts; the other says “too hard” and walks away. This kural says that is the whole difference between a big person and a small one — not how they look, just which one starts climbing.
university_explanation: The couplet is built as a chiasmus, with “seyarkariya” (things difficult to do) standing at the head of both halves so that the same object divides humanity into two classes. What is striking is the definition's austerity: Valluvar offers no content for greatness at all, no list of virtues, only a functional test. “Periyar” and “siriyar” — the great and the small — are terms he uses throughout the Kural as a moral rather than a social ranking, and here he strips them of every birth-based or wealth-based criterion. In context the difficult things are the ascetic disciplines named in the surrounding verses: quenching the senses, discerning the two worlds, holding anger. Later Tamil tradition, reading the chapter alongside yogic literature, glossed the “hard things” as the eight limbs of yoga from yama through samadhi. The verse's blunt symmetry has made it one of the most-quoted couplets in Tamil, routinely cited well outside any ascetic context.

tamil:
சுவைஒளி ஊறுஓசை நாற்றமென்று ஐந்தின்
வகைதெரிவான் கட்டே உலகு.
transliteration:
Suvaiyoli oorosai naatramendru aindhin,
Vakaitherivaan katte ulagu.
current_meaning: The world lies within the grasp of the one who has thoroughly understood the nature of the five — taste, sight, touch, sound and smell.
elementary_explanation: Everything you know about the world came in through five doors: what you taste, see, feel, hear and smell. This kural says the person who really understands those five doors — how they work and how they fool you — is the one who has the whole world figured out.
university_explanation: Valluvar lists the five not as organs but as their objects — suvai (taste), oli (light or form), ooru (touch), osai (sound), naatram (smell) — which is the classical Indian tanmatra scheme, each sense-object paired with one of the five elements. The operative phrase is “vakai therivaan,” the one who discerns the kinds, and “kattu” means a bond, a grip, or a thing held fast: the world is in his hold. Commentators split productively here. Parimelazhagar reads it epistemically — the one who analyses the sense-modes comprehends the world, since the world is nothing but what arrives through them. Others, including modern commentators like Salomon Pappaiah, read it practically — the one who has severed the desires arising through the five has the world at his command. Both readings depend on the same underlying premise, which is arrestingly close to later phenomenology: the world is not encountered apart from the five channels, so mastery of the channels is mastery of the world.

tamil:
நிறைமொழி மாந்தர் பெருமை நிலத்து
மறைமொழி காட்டி விடும்.
transliteration:
Niraimozhi maandhar perumai nilaththu,
Maraimozhi kaatti vidum.
current_meaning: The greatness of those whose words carry their full power is made plain on earth by the sacred sayings they have left behind.
elementary_explanation: Some people say things that just stay true, long after they have gone — you can still hear them repeated hundreds of years later. This kural says you do not need to have met such a person to know how great they were; the words they left behind tell you.
university_explanation: The couplet turns on a pair of near-rhyming compounds. “Nirai-mozhi” is full speech — words so complete that what they say comes about; “marai-mozhi” is hidden or sacred speech, the mantra, the word set apart. Valluvar's claim is evidential: the greatness of such people is not something we take on trust but something the surviving sayings “kaatti vidum,” show up, display, on the earth (“nilaththu”). The verse encodes an old South Asian doctrine of the efficacious utterance — the satya-vakya or act of truth, in which a perfected person's word alters reality because it proceeds from a life that contains no falsehood. What is distinctly Valluvar's is the inversion: rather than arguing that great people produce powerful words, he argues from the words back to the people, making the surviving text the standing proof. The line has an obvious reflexivity for a reader holding the Kural itself, and Tamil tradition has not missed it.

tamil:
குணமென்னும் குன்றேறி நின்றார் வெகுளி
கணமேயும் காத்தல் அரிது.
transliteration:
Gunamennum kundreri nindraar veguli,
Kanameyum kaaththal aridhu.
current_meaning: If those who stand on the hill called good character are once roused to anger, the person who provoked them can scarcely be shielded even for an instant.
elementary_explanation: Some people almost never get angry — so if one of them finally does, you know something has gone very wrong. This kural says the anger of a truly good person is like that: rare, and so serious that nobody can protect whoever caused it, not even for a second.
university_explanation: The couplet works by compounding two improbabilities. “Gunam-ennum kundru” — the hill called character — puts the sage at an elevation, and “nindraar,” having stood, stresses that he has held the position; such a person's “veguli,” hot anger, is by definition rare. Against that rarity Valluvar sets “kanam,” the blink of an eye, the smallest unit of Tamil time-reckoning, and the verb “kaaththal,” to guard or protect: even for a kanam the offender cannot be guarded. Commentators read the verse in two compatible ways — as a warning about the objective force of an ascetic's curse, a commonplace of Indian narrative, and as a moral observation that the anger of the habitually gentle is uniquely devastating because it can only mean a real wrong has been done. The verse is also a fine example of Valluvar's economy with sound: gunam / kundru and kanam / kaaththal set up internal echoes that make the couplet memorable in recitation.

tamil:
அந்தணர் என்போர் அறவோர்மற் றெவ்வுயிர்க்கும்
செந்தண்மை பூண்டொழுக லான்.
transliteration:
Andhanar enbor aravormatru evvuyirkkum,
Sendhanmai poondozhuga laan.
current_meaning: Those properly called anthanar are the truly virtuous, because they live wearing an unbroken, gracious compassion toward every living thing.
elementary_explanation: People sometimes think you are important because of the family you were born into. This kural says no: the title of the highest kind of person belongs to whoever treats every living creature — people, animals, everything — with real kindness, all the time.
university_explanation: The chapter's last couplet is also its most socially radical. “Anthanar,” the honorific ordinarily applied to Brahmins, is here redefined by conduct alone: anthanar are “aravor,” the virtuous, and the reason given is grammatical rather than incidental — the whole second line is a causal clause ending in “ozhuga-laan,” because they conduct themselves so. Traditional Tamil etymology reads anthanar as am (beautiful, gracious) + thanmai (coolness), and Valluvar exploits this by giving them “sen-thanmai,” upright or true coolness, a quality of unheated, unfailing graciousness extended to “ev-uyirkkum,” every living thing without exception — a phrase that takes the claim past human society and into the treatment of animals. Nothing about birth, ritual, thread or learning appears. The verse anchors the ahimsa ethic that Valluvar develops at length in the later chapters on compassion (Arul-udaimai) and abstaining from meat (Pulaal maruththal), and it has been a central text in modern Tamil arguments against caste, including in the work of the twentieth-century reform movements.

chapter_title: Assertion of the Strength of Virtue
tamil:
சிறப்புஈனும் செல்வமும் ஈனும் அறத்தினூஉங்கு
ஆக்கம் எவனோ உயிர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Sirappu eenum selvamum eenum araththinooungu,
Aakkam evano uyirkku.
current_meaning: Virtue yields honour and it yields prosperity too; so what greater good than virtue could there possibly be for any living being?
elementary_explanation: Imagine a tree that gives you both shade and fruit — you would not chop it down looking for something better. Doing the right thing is like that tree: it gives you a good name and it gives you good things in life, so there is nothing better to plant.
university_explanation: Valluvar opens the chapter with a rhetorical question rather than a command, staking out the claim that அறம் (aram, virtue/dharma) is not merely one good among many but the most productive of all. The pairing சிறப்பு (sirappu, 'distinction', glossed by the classical commentator Parimelazhagar as வீடுபேறு, liberation) with செல்வம் (selvam, wealth) collapses the usual opposition between otherworldly merit and worldly gain: virtue delivers both. This anticipates the tripartite scheme of aram–porul–inbam (dharma–artha–kama) that structures the Kural itself, and mirrors the classical Indian doctrine that dharma is the root from which artha and kama grow. The unusual archaic form அறத்தினூஉங்கு, with its alapedai (lengthened vowel), is metrically marked and gives the line its emphatic weight.

chapter_title: Assertion of the Strength of Virtue
tamil:
அறத்தினூஉங்கு ஆக்கமும் இல்லை அதனை
மறத்தலின் ஊங்கில்லை கேடு.
transliteration:
Araththinooungu aakkamum illai adhanai,
Maraththalin oongillai kedu.
current_meaning: There is no greater gain than virtue, and there is no greater ruin than forgetting it.
elementary_explanation: Think of brushing your teeth. Doing it is the best thing for your teeth, and forgetting to do it is the worst thing for them. This kural says goodness works the same way — doing it is the best thing possible, and forgetting about it is the worst.
university_explanation: The couplet is built on a deliberate chiasmus: ஆக்கம் (aakkam, increase/gain) is set against கேடு (kedu, ruin/loss), and the pivot between them is not 'doing evil' but மறத்தல் (marathal, forgetting). Valluvar's diagnosis of moral failure is therefore cognitive rather than volitional — Parimelazhagar glosses the forgetting as arising from மயக்கம் (delusion), not defiance. This makes the verse subtly different from ordinary two-path moralism: the opposite of virtue is not vice but inattention. The verse also repeats அறத்தினூஉங்கு from Kural 31, a rhetorical device (antadi-like linkage) binding the chapter's opening pair into a single argument.

chapter_title: Assertion of the Strength of Virtue
tamil:
ஒல்லும் வகையான் அறவினை ஓவாதே
செல்லும்வாய் எல்லாஞ் செயல்.
transliteration:
Ollum vakaiyaan aravinai ovaadhe,
Sellumvaai ellaanj cheyal.
current_meaning: By whatever means you are able, without ever letting up, do good in every situation where good can be done.
elementary_explanation: You do not need to be strong to help. If you can carry one book, carry one book. This kural says: do whatever good you can manage, wherever you happen to be, and do not stop.
university_explanation: Three qualifiers do the work here. ஒல்லும் வகையான் ('by the means available to you') scales the obligation to individual capacity — Parimelazhagar specifies that the householder gives according to his means and the ascetic according to his bodily strength. ஓவாதே ('without ceasing') removes any notion of virtue as an occasional act. செல்லும்வாய் எல்லாம् ('in every place it can reach') is glossed by the commentators as the three instruments of mind, speech and body (மனம், வாக்கு, காயம்), yielding good thought, good word and good deed. The verse thus converts virtue from a discrete achievement into a continuous disposition, and does so without ever specifying a quantity — a characteristically Tamil ethical move that keeps the demand universal and the standard personal.

chapter_title: Assertion of the Strength of Virtue
tamil:
மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன் ஆதல் அனைத்தறன்
ஆகுல நீர பிற.
transliteration:
Manaththukkan maasilan aadhal anaiththu aran,
Aakula neera pira.
current_meaning: To be free of stain in the mind — that alone is virtue; everything else is mere noise and display.
elementary_explanation: You can wash the outside of a cup and still leave it dirty inside, and nobody would want to drink from it. This kural says goodness is about being clean on the inside; showing off on the outside is just noise.
university_explanation: This is one of the Kural's most radical reductions: அனைத்து அறன் — 'that is the whole of virtue' — locates morality entirely in மனத்துக்கண் மாசு, stain in the mind. The dismissive ஆகுல நீர ('of the nature of clamour') is aimed, on Manakkudavar's reading, at conduct performed so that others will notice it; Parimelazhagar extends it to outward religious garb (வேடம்) and pious talk. Coming immediately after a verse commanding ceaseless outward action, Kural 34 prevents that command from collapsing into ritualism, and it prepares the ground for Kural 35's inventory of specifically mental vices. The move parallels — but does not derive from — the Jain and Buddhist emphasis on cetanā (intention) as the locus of karma, and is one reason the Kural has been read as compatible with renunciant and householder ethics alike.

chapter_title: Assertion of the Strength of Virtue
tamil:
அழுக்காறு அவாவெகுளி இன்னாச்சொல் நான்கும்
இழுக்கா இயன்றது அறம்.
transliteration:
Azhukkaaru avaavekuli innaachchol naankum,
Izhukkaa iyandradhu aram.
current_meaning: Conduct that keeps clear of all four — envy, greed, anger and harsh speech — and goes on steadily: that is virtue.
elementary_explanation: Four things spoil a good day: wanting what your friend has, wanting more and more for yourself, losing your temper, and saying something mean. This kural says being good mostly means steering around those four.
university_explanation: Valluvar here gives virtue a negative definition — a via negativa built from four named faults, each of which will later receive its own chapter or sub-treatment in the Kural. அழுக்காறு (envy at another's prosperity), அவா (craving running out through the senses), வெகுளி (the anger that erupts when craving is blocked) and இன்னாச்சொல் (the harsh word that anger produces) are arranged by Parimelazhagar as a causal chain rather than a list, so the four are really one process caught at four stages. The verbal form இழுக்கா ('not slipping') is a negative participle drawn from the vocabulary of footing and balance, so the image is of walking a path without stumbling. Note the textual crux: some manuscripts and a persistent popular tradition read ஈயாமை (miserliness) in place of நான்கும், but the reading with நான்கும் is the one carried by the major commentarial tradition and by the standard printed editions used here.

chapter_title: Assertion of the Strength of Virtue
tamil:
அன்றறிவாம் என்னாது அறஞ்செய்க மற்றது
பொன்றுங்கால் பொன்றாத் துணை.
transliteration:
Andrarivaam ennaadhu aranjeyka matradhu,
Pondrungaal pondraath thunai.
current_meaning: Do not say 'we will see to it when the time comes' — do good now; for when you perish, that alone will be the companion that does not perish.
elementary_explanation: If you keep saying you will pack your bag tomorrow, one day the bus leaves without you. This kural says do good things today, because they are the only things that stay with you when everything else is gone.
university_explanation: The idiom அன்றறிவாம் — literally 'we shall know on that day' — is the voice of procrastination personified; Parimelazhagar expands it as the young person's reasoning, 'we are young now, we will do it at the hour of death.' Against this Valluvar sets the wordplay that gives the couplet its force: பொன்றுங்கால் பொன்றாத் துணை, 'at the time of perishing, the unperishing companion', built on repetition of the root பொன்று- in opposite senses. The image of virtue as துணை (companion, escort) that accompanies the soul past the body's dissolution is shared with Jain and Buddhist merit-doctrine, and Manakkudavar reads it explicitly as support in the next birth; the Dravidian rationalist commentator Kalaignar Karunanidhi instead reads it as imperishable fame. The verse is one of the clearest places where the Kural's deliberate theological reticence allows two very different readings of the same line.

chapter_title: Assertion of the Strength of Virtue
tamil:
அறத்தாறு இதுவென வேண்டா சிவிகை
பொறுத்தானோடு ஊர்ந்தான் இடை.
transliteration:
Araththaaru ithuvena ventaa sivikai,
Poruththaanotu oorndhaan itai.
current_meaning: There is no need for anyone to expound what the fruit of virtue is: just look at the difference between the man carrying the palanquin and the man riding in it.
elementary_explanation: Some things you do not need explained — you just look. Two people are on the same road: one is carrying the chair, one is sitting in it. This kural says the difference between doing good and not doing good shows up like that, plain to see.
university_explanation: This is the Kural's most striking piece of epistemology. Parimelazhagar reads the verse in the technical vocabulary of Indian logic: there is no need for ஆகம அளவை (scriptural testimony, verbal authority) because காட்சி அளவை (pratyakṣa, direct perception) settles the matter. Valluvar is arguing that karmic consequence is empirically visible in the unequal fortunes of the palanquin-bearer and the palanquin-rider, an argument for virtue that requires no revelation. The verse has also been the chapter's most contested: modern readers, including Kalaignar Karunanidhi in his widely read commentary, have resisted the implication that social inequality is morally deserved, and reinterpret the pair as contrasting inner ease with inner burden rather than birth-station. Either way the rhetorical claim stands — the strength of virtue is a matter of observation, not argument.

chapter_title: Assertion of the Strength of Virtue
tamil:
வீழ்நாள் படாஅமை நன்றாற்றின் அஃதொருவன்
வாழ்நாள் வழியடைக்கும் கல்.
transliteration:
Veezhnaal pataaamai nandraatrin aqdhoruvan,
Vaazhnaal vazhiyataikkum kal.
current_meaning: If a person does good without letting a single day fall away empty, that practice becomes the stone that blocks the road by which further births would come.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a gate that keeps swinging open, and every day you do a good thing you push a stone a little closer to it. Do it every single day and eventually the stone sits right in the gateway and the gate cannot open again.
university_explanation: The couplet turns on two metaphors that must be held together. வீழ்நாள் — a 'fallen day', a day let slip without good done — is set against கல், a blocking stone. Parimelazhagar reads வாழ்நாள் வழி as the road by which embodied life keeps recurring, so the daily practice of aram literally walls up the passage of rebirth; he glosses the whole verse as the statement that virtue yields வீடு (liberation), and imports the five kleśas of the Sanskrit tradition to explain what keeps the road open. The image of blocking rather than escaping is unusual and concrete — the Kural does not speak of transcending the cycle but of obstructing it, as one blocks a cattle-track with a boulder. Modern rationalist commentators such as Kalaignar Karunanidhi, resisting the rebirth reading, take கல் instead as a paving-stone that smooths the road of one's own life.

chapter_title: Assertion of the Strength of Virtue
tamil:
அறத்தான் வருவதே இன்பம் மற்றெல்லாம்
புறத்த புகழும் இல.
transliteration:
Araththaan varuvadhe inpam matrellaam,
Puraththa pukazhum ila.
current_meaning: Only what comes by way of virtue is genuine pleasure; everything else falls outside pleasure altogether, and carries no honour either.
elementary_explanation: Winning a game by cheating does not really feel like winning, and nobody claps for it. This kural says the only fun that is truly fun is the kind you got the right way.
university_explanation: The key word is புறத்த — 'they are outside', i.e. outside the category of இன்பம் (inbam, pleasure) altogether. Valluvar is not saying illicit pleasure is a lesser pleasure; he is saying it does not belong to the class at all, and Parimelazhagar completes the logic by noting that what lies outside pleasure is துன்பம், pain. The second clause adds a social criterion: such gains are also புகழும் இல, devoid of honour. Reading the verse against the third book of the Kural, the காமத்துப்பால் devoted entirely to erotic love, shows that Valluvar is not renouncing pleasure but defining its legitimate channel; Parimelazhagar accordingly glosses அறத்தான் as இல்லறத்தோடு பொருந்தி, 'in accordance with domestic virtue'. The verse thus quietly integrates the three aims of life rather than ranking them.

chapter_title: Assertion of the Strength of Virtue
tamil:
செயற்பால தோரும் அறனே ஒருவற்கு
உயற்பால தோரும் பழி.
transliteration:
Seyarpaala thorum arane oruvarku,
Uyarpaala thorum pazhi.
current_meaning: What a person ought to do is, in every case, virtue; what a person ought to avoid is, in every case, what deserves blame.
elementary_explanation: There are only two piles in life: things to do and things to keep away from. This kural puts everything kind and fair in the first pile, and everything you would be ashamed of in the second.
university_explanation: The chapter closes by compressing its whole argument into a definition. செயற்பால ('the doable', what belongs to the category of what should be done) is equated with அறன், and உயற்பால ('the avoidable') with பழி — blame, or what is blameworthy. The particles ஓரும் are treated by Parimelazhagar as அசைநிலை, metrical fillers carrying no independent sense, while the emphatic ஏ in அறனே is carried over to the second line by implication, making both halves exclusive. Manakkudavar adds a pointed reason for placing this verse last: Kural 38 had promised that virtue blocks rebirth, and a reader might suppose that good deeds could simply be added on top of bad ones — so Valluvar closes by insisting that the avoidance of blame is as constitutive of the definition as the doing of good. Notably, Valluvar chooses பழி (blame) rather than a word for sin, keeping his ethics answerable to public judgement rather than to divine law.

tamil:
இல்வாழ்வான் என்பான் இயல்புடைய மூவர்க்கும்
நல்லாற்றின் நின்ற துணை.
transliteration:
Ilvaazhvaan enpaan iyalputaiya moovarkkum,
Nallaatrin nindra thunai.
current_meaning: The one who truly deserves the name “householder” is the steady support, along the path of virtue, of the three others who depend on him.
elementary_explanation: Think of a family like a table. The person who runs the household is the tabletop — everyone else rests on it. Parents, partner, children (and in the old way of counting, students, hermits, and wandering monks) all lean on the householder, and a good householder holds them all up and keeps them going the right way.
university_explanation: The chapter that opens the இல்லறவியல் (illaraviyal, “the way of domestic virtue”) begins by defining the householder functionally rather than sentimentally: he is a துணை (thunai, “support/companion/prop”) who stands நல்லாற்றின் (nallaatrin, “in the good way”). Commentators split sharply on who the “three” (மூவர்) are. Parimelazhagar and the older Sanskritising tradition read them as the other three ashramas — brahmacharin, vanaprastha and sannyasin — aligning the verse with Manu's grihastha doctrine; Kalaignar Karunanidhi and Salomon Pappaiah read them domestically as parents, spouse and children (or children, parents and kin). Valluvar's deliberate vagueness lets both readings stand, which is characteristic of his non-sectarian method. The crucial word is நின்ற (nindra, “having stood firm”) — not occasional charity but a standing, load-bearing role, and the standing must be *on the right path*, so that support which enables wrongdoing does not count.

tamil:
துறந்தார்க்கும் துவ்வாதவர்க்கும் இறந்தார்க்கும்
இல்வாழ்வான் என்பான் துணை.
transliteration:
Thurandhaarkkum thuvvaadhavarkkum irandhaarkkum,
Ilvaazhvaan enpaan thunai.
current_meaning: The householder is the support of those who have renounced the world, of those who have nothing to eat, and of those who have died.
elementary_explanation: Imagine one family in a village that keeps a pot of rice always ready. The travelling monk who owns nothing eats from it. The hungry neighbour eats from it. And a share is set aside in memory of grandparents who have died. That one household quietly feeds three groups who cannot feed themselves.
university_explanation: Valluvar names three classes with three neat participial nouns: துறந்தார் (thurandhaar, “those who have let go”), துவ்வாதவர் (thuvvaadhavar, literally “those who do not eat” — the destitute), and இறந்தார் (irandhaar, “those who have passed”). The last is the most striking to a modern reader: the dead are treated as an ongoing claim on the living, through the memorial offerings (தென்புலத்தார் rites) that the next couplet will name explicitly. The verse is a deliberate argumentative move within a Tamil intellectual landscape in which Jain and Buddhist renunciant ideals were culturally prestigious: Valluvar concedes the renunciant's standing and then points out that the renunciant literally eats because a householder cooked. Economic dependency becomes a moral argument for the dignity of domestic life.

tamil:
தென்புலத்தார் தெய்வம் விருந்தொக்கல் தானென்றாங்கு
ஐம்புலத்தாறு ஓம்பல் தலை.
transliteration:
Thenpulaththaar theyvam virundhokkal thaanendraangu,
Aimpulaththaaru ompal thalai.
current_meaning: The householder's foremost duty is to cherish, in due measure, five claims: the departed ancestors, the gods, guests, kinfolk, and oneself.
elementary_explanation: A good household is like a table set with five plates. One is for the grandparents who have passed away, one is for God, one for whoever knocks at the door, one for the family, and one for yourself. Forgetting any plate — including your own — means the table isn't really set.
university_explanation: This is the Kural's compressed version of the fivefold domestic obligation. தென்புலத்தார் (thenpulaththaar) literally means “those of the southern region” — the dead, since the south is Yama's quarter — and is the standard Tamil term for the ancestors (pitṛ). The other four are தெய்வம் (theyvam, the gods), விருந்து (virundhu, the guest — a theme Valluvar gives a whole chapter to at 9), ஒக்கல் (okkal, kin), and தான் (thaan, oneself). The inclusion of *oneself* is philosophically important: Valluvar's domestic ethic is not self-erasing asceticism but a balanced distribution, captured by ஓம்பல் (ombal, “to cherish/tend/guard”) and by தலை (thalai, “the head, the foremost thing”). The scheme corresponds closely to the Brahminical pañca-mahāyajña, but Valluvar strips it of ritual technicality and states it as household budgeting of love and resources.

tamil:
பழியஞ்சிப் பாத்தூண் உடைத்தாயின் வாழ்க்கை
வழியெஞ்சல் எஞ்ஞான்றும் இல்.
transliteration:
Pazhiyanjip paaththoon utaiththaayin vaazhkkai,
Vazhiyenjal egngnaandrum il.
current_meaning: If a household shuns blame in how it earns and shares out what it eats, its line will never fail, in any age.
elementary_explanation: Suppose a family grows apples honestly and always gives some away to neighbours. Everyone keeps trading with them, everyone helps them in a bad year, and the orchard keeps going for generations. A family that steals its apples and eats them alone soon has neither friends nor orchard.
university_explanation: Two conditions are compressed into one line: பழியஞ்சி (pazhi-anji, “fearing blame/reproach”) governs *acquisition*, and பாத்தூண் (paath-ūṇ, from பகுத்து உண்ணல், “eating after apportioning”) governs *consumption*. The reward is stated negatively and absolutely: வழி எஞ்சல் … இல் — “there is never a failing of the line.” வழி (vazhi) means both “way” and “lineage,” so the promise is simultaneously that the household's path and its descendants will not run out. Note that Valluvar's ethical lever here is பழி (pazhi, public blame) rather than sin — an honour-and-reproach vocabulary rooted in Tamil Sangam social ethics rather than in a theology of divine punishment, which is part of why the Kural reads as secular to modern audiences.

tamil:
அன்பும் அறனும் உடைத்தாயின் இல்வாழ்க்கை
பண்பும் பயனும் அது.
transliteration:
Anpum aranum utaiththaayin ilvaazhkkai,
Panpum payanum adhu.
current_meaning: If domestic life possesses love and virtue, then that possession is at once its true character and its whole reward.
elementary_explanation: Think of a fruit tree that is both beautiful and gives fruit. You don't grow it for some other prize somewhere else — the tree being what it is *is* the prize. A home with love and goodness in it is the same: it is not a step toward the good life, it already is the good life.
university_explanation: The verse turns on a deliberate identity statement: பண்பும் பயனும் அது — “its quality and its fruit are *that*.” Valluvar collapses the usual ethical distinction between a virtue and the reward the virtue earns. அன்பு (anpu, love) and அறன் (aran, virtue/dharma) are not instruments for obtaining household happiness; they *constitute* it. This is a genuinely Aristotelian move — the household, rightly constituted, is an end in itself, not a means — and it is what allows Valluvar in the following verses to argue that the householder need not look elsewhere (46) and outranks the ascetic (48). அன்பு gets a full chapter later (8, அன்புடைமை); here it is paired with அறன் so that affection alone is not enough, nor correctness alone.

tamil:
அறத்தாற்றின் இல்வாழ்க்கை ஆற்றின் புறத்தாற்றில்
போஒய்ப் பெறுவ தெவன்?
transliteration:
Araththaatrin ilvaazhkkai aatrin puraththaatril,
Pooip peruva thevan?
current_meaning: If a person conducts domestic life along the path of virtue, what more is there to be gained by going off to some other path?
elementary_explanation: If the water in your own well is clean and cold, why walk ten miles to another village's well? The answer is: there's no reason to. Living well at home already gives you what you would go looking for elsewhere.
university_explanation: The couplet is framed as a rhetorical question — பெறுவது எவன்? (“what is there to obtain?”) — and the expected answer is “nothing.” புறத்தாற்றில் (puraththaatril, “on the outside path”) is the polite euphemism for the ascetic's road, the துறவறம் that Valluvar treats sympathetically in chapters 3 and 35. The argument is not that renunciation is false but that it is redundant *for someone already doing the domestic path properly*, the operative qualifier being அறத்தாற்றின் (“by the way of virtue”). Note the doubled ஆறு/ஆற்று root — path, path, outside-path — which makes the verse a small meditation on the metaphor of the road itself. This is the pivot on which the whole chapter, and arguably the whole of Book I's householder section, turns.

tamil:
இயல்பினான் இல்வாழ்க்கை வாழ்பவன் என்பான்
முயல்வாருள் எல்லாம் தலை.
transliteration:
Iyalpinaan ilvaazhkkai vaazhpavan enpaan,
Muyalvaarul ellaam thalai.
current_meaning: The one who lives domestic life according to its proper nature stands at the head of all who strive for the good.
elementary_explanation: In a race, lots of people train in fancy ways. But the one who simply runs correctly, step after step, finishes first. The person who does ordinary family life properly is that runner — ahead of everyone who is trying harder in more dramatic ways.
university_explanation: The decisive word is இயல்பினான் (iyalpinaan) — “by [its] nature,” the same root as இயல்புடைய in kural 41. Valluvar is not praising domestic life as such but domestic life lived *according to what it intrinsically is*, which chapters 41-46 have just specified: support of dependants, the fivefold obligation, blameless earning, shared food, love and virtue. Against that, முயல்வாருள் எல்லாம் தலை — “the head of all who exert themselves” — uses முயல் (muyal, to strive/labour), a word that in the religious register covers ascetic exertion and spiritual practice. The claim is competitive and startling for its time: the householder is not merely an acceptable alternative to the striving religious, he outranks them. Parimelazhagar's commentary reads this as Valluvar explicitly ranking இல்லறம் above துறவறம்.

tamil:
ஆற்றின் ஒழுக்கி அறனிழுக்கா இல்வாழ்க்கை
நோற்பாரின் நோன்மை உடைத்து.
transliteration:
Aatrin ozhukki aranizhukkaa ilvaazhkkai,
Norpaarin nonmai utaiththu.
current_meaning: A domestic life that keeps others moving along the right path and never itself slips from virtue has greater strength than the austerities of those who do penance.
elementary_explanation: One person sits alone on a hill and eats nothing for a week — that's hard. Another person gets up every day, stays honest, feeds the family, and gently keeps everyone else honest too — for fifty years. This kural says the second one is doing the harder, stronger thing.
university_explanation: The verse builds a careful two-part condition before making its comparison. ஆற்றின் ஒழுக்கி (aatrin ozhukki) is causative — “having caused [others] to conduct themselves on the path” — while அறனிழுக்கா (aran-izhukkaa) is negative and reflexive: “not itself slipping from virtue.” Only a household meeting both conditions is then said to possess நோன்மை (nonmai) exceeding that of நோற்பார் (norpaar, those who undertake நோன்பு, austerity/penance). The pun is the point: நோன்மை means both “endurance under penance” and “strength,” so Valluvar claims the householder wins the ascetic's own contest on the ascetic's own metric. This is the chapter's most polemical line and reflects a broader Tamil bhakti-era and post-Sangam argument against Jain and Buddhist monastic prestige.

tamil:
அறனெனப் பட்டதே இல்வாழ்க்கை அஃதும்
பிறன்பழிப்ப தில்லாயின் நன்று.
transliteration:
Aran enap pattadhe ilvaazhkkai aqdhum,
Piranpazhippa thillaayin nandru.
current_meaning: What has properly been called virtue is domestic life itself; and the other way of life too is good, provided no one has cause to reproach it.
elementary_explanation: Imagine someone asks, "What does 'being good' actually mean?" This kural answers: it means running a home well. And it adds, politely, that the other way — going off to be a monk — is fine too, as long as nobody can point at it and say something is wrong.
university_explanation: The emphatic particle in அறனெனப் பட்டதே (aran-enap-pattadhē, “the very thing that has been called virtue”) is a definitional claim: domestic life is not *a* form of aram, it is what the word names. The second half is one of the Kural's most gracious sentences — அஃதும் (“that too”) concedes the ascetic path, but hedges it with a condition (பிறன் பழிப்பது இல்லாயின், “if there is nothing for another to reproach”) that Valluvar never attaches to the householder. Commentators differ over whether அஃதும் refers to the renunciant life or to a second grade of domestic life; the majority reading, followed by Mu. Varadarajan and Salomon Pappaiah, takes it as the ascetic path. Note the recurrence of பழி (pazhi, blame) from kural 44 — reproachability is Valluvar's working test for ethical failure throughout this chapter.

tamil:
வையத்துள் வாழ்வாங்கு வாழ்பவன் வான்உறையும்
தெய்வத்துள் வைக்கப் படும்.
transliteration:
Vaiyaththul vaazhvaangu vaazhpavan vaanuraiyum,
Theyvaththul vaikkap padum.
current_meaning: Whoever lives on this earth in the way one ought to live will be reckoned among the gods who dwell in the sky.
elementary_explanation: You don't have to go anywhere special to become great. If you live rightly here — kindly, honestly, taking care of people — the world will think of you the way it thinks of the shining beings in the sky. Being good on the ground is what puts you up there.
university_explanation: The chapter's closing couplet is built on a deliberate spatial contrast: வையத்துள் (vaiyaththul, “within the world/earth”) against வான் உறையும் (vaan uraiyum, “sky-dwelling”). The pivot is the untranslatable வாழ்வாங்கு வாழ்பவன் — “one who lives in the manner of living,” i.e. one who lives as living is properly done. The passive வைக்கப்படும் (vaikkap-padum, “will be placed/reckoned”) is carefully non-supernatural: Valluvar does not say such a person *becomes* a god or *goes* to heaven, but that he will be *counted among* them — an evaluative rather than metaphysical claim, which is why the verse has been read comfortably by Saiva, Vaishnava, Jain and secular-humanist commentators alike. It is also the structural answer to kural 1: the book opened by putting God first; it closes this chapter by putting the good householder alongside the gods.

tamil:
மனைத்தக்க மாண்புடையள் ஆகித்தற் கொண்டான்
வளத்தக்காள் வாழ்க்கைத் துணை.
transliteration:
Manaith thakka maanbudaiyaL aagith thaR koNdaan,
vaLath thakkaaL vaazhkkaith thuNai.
current_meaning: She who possesses the excellences that household life requires, and who orders that life to match the means of the man who married her, is a true life-partner.
elementary_explanation: Imagine two people rowing one boat. It only moves straight if they pull together with the strength each of them actually has — not with strength they wish they had. This kural says a good partner is the one who runs the home well and spends what the family really earns, not what it pretends to earn.
university_explanation: Valluvar opens the chapter with a definition rather than a eulogy, and the definition is startlingly practical: the wife's worth is located in maanbu (moral excellence fitted to the household) plus vaLaththakkaaL — living proportionate to income. Parimelazhagar's classical commentary glosses the "good qualities" as hospitality to ascetics and guests and compassion to the poor, and the "good deeds" as knowing what the household needs, competence in the kitchen, and oppuravu (civic generosity) — so domestic thrift is framed not as miserliness but as the material precondition of ethical generosity established in Chapter 5 (Il-vaazhkkai). The chapter's title is also significant: Valluvar does not call it "manaiviyin maanbu" (the greatness of a wife) but vaazhkkaith-thuNai nalam, "the worth of a life-companion," a word choice Tamil commentators have long read as elevating the wife from an object of the household to its co-agent. Modern feminist readings of the Kural note the asymmetry — the chapter addresses the wife's duties to a far greater extent than the husband's — while also observing that Valluvar's criterion is competence and character rather than birth, beauty, or dowry, which was itself a notable move in the ancient Tamil context.

tamil:
மனைமாட்சி இல்லாள்கண் இல்லாயின் வாழ்க்கை
எனைமாட்சித் தாயினும் இல்.
transliteration:
Manaimaatchi illaaLkaN illaayin vaazhkkai,
enaimaatchith thaayinum il.
current_meaning: If the wife lacks the excellence that household life requires, then however much splendour a man's life may otherwise possess, it amounts to nothing.
elementary_explanation: A house can have the shiniest roof, the biggest garden and the nicest furniture — but if the roof leaks, none of the rest keeps you dry. This kural says the wife's goodness is the roof: if it's missing, everything else stops counting.
university_explanation: The rhetorical engine here is the word il, which Valluvar uses twice in different senses — il as 'home/household' and il as 'is not, amounts to nothing' — so the couplet ends on the flat negation that domestic splendour without domestic virtue simply is not. Parimelazhagar notes precisely this, glossing the final il as meaning 'useless', not 'absent'. The Tamil didactic tradition amplified the point: the Naaladiyaar declares that a mansion with jewelled lamps but no worthy mistress is 'a cruel forest', an image the anthologist of this chapter explicitly quotes. Comparative scholars often pair this couplet with the near-universal wisdom-literature topos that a household's moral weather is set by the spouse rather than by its wealth — a topos with strikingly parallel formulations in Hebrew Proverbs, Hesiod, and the Pali canon. It should be noted that Valluvar states the principle asymmetrically here; the Kural does address husbandly failure elsewhere (notably Chapter 91, Penvazhich cheral), but this chapter's frame is the wife's contribution.

tamil:
இல்லதென் இல்லவள் மாண்பானால் உள்ளதென்
இல்லவள் மாணாக் கடை.
transliteration:
Illadhen illavaL maaNbaanaal uLLadhen,
illavaL maaNaak kadai.
current_meaning: If the wife of the house is truly excellent, what does a man lack? And if she is not, what does he actually possess?
elementary_explanation: Think of a key. If you have the right key, every locked door in the house opens — so nothing is really shut to you. Lose the key and it doesn't matter how many rooms you own; you can't get into any of them. This kural says a good partner is that key.
university_explanation: The couplet is built as a matched pair of rhetorical questions — illadhu en? ('what is lacking?') against uLLadhu en? ('what is there?') — and the symmetry is the argument: presence and absence of wifely maaNbu are made to exhaust the possibilities, with nothing in between. This antithetical-parallelism structure is a signature of Near Eastern and Tamil wisdom poetry alike, and it produces here a deliberately absolute claim that later Tamil moralists softened or literalised in various directions; Avvaiyar's Moodhurai rewrites it as the image of a house turning into a sour thicket. Parimelazhagar's note that maaNbu, an abstract quality-noun, stands here for the person who has it is an important grammatical observation — Valluvar is not praising an attribute detachable from the woman but identifying her with it. Read together, Kurals 52 and 53 form a diptych: 52 denies that external goods can substitute for her, 53 denies that anything remains once she is subtracted. Comparative scholarship frequently notes that Proverbs 12:4 states the identical antithesis in a single verse, and the Tamil commentarial tradition itself has cited that biblical parallel since at least the nineteenth century.

tamil:
பெண்ணின் பெருந்தக்க யாவுள கற்பென்னும்
திண்மைஉண் டாகப் பெறின்.
transliteration:
PeNNin perundhakka yaavuLa kaRpennum,
thiNmai uNdaagap peRin.
current_meaning: If a woman possesses the inner firmness called karpu — steadfast fidelity of mind — what greater treasure is there in the world than she is?
elementary_explanation: Some things are strong because they are heavy, like a rock. Other things are strong because they don't bend, like a steel bar. This kural is about the second kind of strength — the inside kind, where a person decides something and simply never wobbles. It says nothing you could own is worth more than a partner like that.
university_explanation: The pivotal term is thiNmai — hardness, firmness, tensile strength — which Valluvar applies to karpu, and the metaphor is deliberate: karpu is not presented as a restriction imposed from outside but as a structural property of the person, a kalangaa nilaimai (unshakeable state) in Parimelazhagar's phrase. This matters because karpu is one of the most contested words in Tamil literary history: Tolkappiyam already ranks it above naaN (modesty), the Silappatikaram builds its entire tragic architecture on Kannagi's karpu as a force capable of burning a city, and modern Tamil feminist criticism (from Periyarist writing onward) has extensively critiqued the way karpu was later narrowed into a purely sexual and purely female obligation. Valluvar's own usage here is notably psychological rather than juridical — thiNmai is a quality of mind, and the next couplet's imagery of cosmic power flows from it. Comparative readers should note that nearly every tradition surveyed in this chapter has a 'her price is above rubies' formula, but relatively few, like Valluvar, locate the value explicitly in an interior strength rather than in outward conduct or reputation.

tamil:
தெய்வம் தொழாஅள் கொழுநன் தொழுதெழுவாள்
பெய்யெனப் பெய்யும் மழை.
transliteration:
Theyvam thozhaaaL kozhunan thozhudhezhuvaaL,
peyyenap peyyum mazhai.
current_meaning: She who worships no other god but reveres her husband as she rises each day — if she says 'rain', the rain will fall.
elementary_explanation: This is a very old saying about how powerful someone's devotion was believed to be: so powerful that even the clouds would listen. People used to tell stories like this to show that a promise kept perfectly gives a person a kind of strength the world has to respect. Today many people read it differently — and disagree with it — which is worth knowing too.
university_explanation: This is the most contested couplet in the chapter and arguably in Book I. Read plainly it asserts that a wife's exclusive devotion to her husband confers thaumaturgic power over nature — a claim with deep roots in Tamil literature, where Kannagi's karpu incinerates Madurai and the chaste woman's word commands the elements. Parimelazhagar reads it straightforwardly as establishing 'the power of the woman of karpu' (kaRpudaiyavaLadhu aatral). But modern readings diverge sharply: M. Karunanidhi's widely circulated commentary renders the couplet critically, treating the woman who worships her husband as god as one who has reduced herself to servitude, while other scholars argue the couplet is hyperbolic praise of moral force rather than a prescription of husband-worship, and still others note that Valluvar's own Chapter 1 pointedly refuses sectarian deity-worship, so 'thozhaaaL theyvam' may be less about theology than about single-pointed commitment. The comparative material below shows that the specific motif — a devoted wife's prayer bringing rain — appears independently in the Babylonian Talmud, which is a remarkable convergence. The honest scholarly position is that the couplet encodes a genuinely asymmetric marital theology that many readers today reject while still finding the underlying claim about the force of integrity intelligible.

tamil:
தற்காத்துத் தற்கொண்டாற் பேணித் தகைசான்ற
சொற்காத்துச் சோர்விலாள் பெண்.
transliteration:
ThaRkaaththuth thaRkoNdaaR peaNith thagaisaandra,
soRkaaththuch soarvilaaL peN.
current_meaning: She who guards herself, cherishes the man who married her, keeps the household's good name unblemished, and never slackens in any of it — she is what 'wife' truly means.
elementary_explanation: Think of someone holding three things at once — their own promise, their partner, and the family's good name — and never letting any of the three drop, not even when they're tired. This kural says that's not just a nice thing to do; that's what the word 'wife' actually means.
university_explanation: Structurally this is a definition-by-enumeration, listing four duties and then delivering the predicate in a single final word: peN. Valluvar's three objects of guarding move outward in concentric circles — thaR-kaaththu (guarding the self), thaR-koNdaan peaNi (tending the one who took her), soR-kaaththu (guarding the word, i.e. reputation) — and the fourth term, soarvu-ilaaL ('she in whom there is no slackening'), converts them from acts into a sustained disposition; Parimelazhagar glosses soarvu as maRavi, forgetfulness or lapse, making constancy of attention the operative virtue. The word soL here is usually read by commentators as puhaz, the spoken good name that a village confers, which locates a significant part of wifely virtue in the social rather than the private sphere.
