Tamil tradition has long linked this couplet to Vasuki Ammaiyar, Valluvar's legendary wife, and the anthologists of this chapter pair it with a line from the deuterocanonical Ben Sira on the doubled days of a good wife's husband. Note also the quiet reciprocity implied: the kural says 'the man who took her' (thaR-koNdaan), keeping the marriage contractual and two-sided even while the duties enumerated are hers.

tamil:
சிறைகாக்கும் காப்பெவன் செய்யும் மகளிர்
நிறைகாக்கும் காப்பே தலை.
transliteration:
SiRaikaakkum kaappevan seyyum magaLir,
niRaikaakkum kaappe thalai.
current_meaning: What can confinement and surveillance ever accomplish? The only guard worth having is the guard women keep over themselves through their own inner steadiness.
elementary_explanation: You can't make a plant grow by building a cage around it — the growing happens inside the plant or it doesn't happen at all. This kural says the same about being good: locking someone up doesn't make them trustworthy. Only the choice they make inside themselves does.
university_explanation: This couplet is one of the strongest statements of moral autonomy anywhere in ancient world literature, and its force depends on a precise contrast between two words for 'guarding': siRai (an enclosure — the word covers a dam, a fortress wall, a prison) and niRai (fullness, the mind held steady in its own course). Parimelazhagar spells out the mechanism — siRai means walls and gatekeepers, niRai means 'setting the heart firm in the way of karpu' — and concludes that without the latter the former produces nothing, which is why Valluvar writes kaappe with the exclusive particle. The couplet is frequently cited in modern Tamil discourse as evidence that Valluvar opposed the seclusion of women, and it is genuinely difficult to read otherwise: the opening is a rhetorical question with a contemptuous edge (evan seyyum — 'what will it do?'). It is also a remarkable convergence with Manusmriti 9.12, which makes the same argument in almost the same words, suggesting a shared ancient Indic debate about the futility of physical guardianship. The obvious limitation, which honest scholarship should name, is that Valluvar's alternative to confinement is internalised self-restraint rather than freedom as such; the couplet dismantles the prison without dismantling the expectation.

tamil:
பெற்றாற் பெறின்பெறுவர் பெண்டிர் பெருஞ்சிறப்புப்
புத்தேளிர் வாழும் உலகு.
transliteration:
PetraaR peRin peRuvar peNdir perunjiRappup,
puththeLir vaazhum ulagu.
current_meaning: Women who faithfully honour the husband they have received will obtain great glory in the world where the celestials dwell.
elementary_explanation: This kural is about a reward that doesn't come in this life. It says that quietly doing right by your family, day after day, with nobody applauding, is the kind of thing that gets remembered in the highest place there is — even if nobody on earth noticed.
university_explanation: The couplet is a masterclass in Tamil sound-patterning — petraaR peRin peRuvar peNdir perunjiRappu stacks five p-initial words in a single line — and Valluvar uses the alliterative momentum to carry the chapter from the domestic to the cosmic register. Parimelazhagar supplies the elided verb (vazhipaduthal, 'reverencing'), giving the standard reading: women who honour their husbands are themselves honoured by the puttheLir (devas). But the couplet is genuinely ambiguous in Tamil, and the divergence in the commentaries is instructive: M. Varadarajan reads it as the wife's reward for duty, while M. Karunanidhi reads petraaR as 'a husband of good character whom she obtains', making the couplet about a woman's good fortune in her marriage rather than her merit in it. Either way, the structural function is clear — after four couplets defining the wife's excellence, Valluvar extends its consequence past death, a move he makes sparingly in the Aram book. The comparative material below is unusually rich here, because nearly every tradition surveyed developed an explicit doctrine of otherworldly recompense for the faithful wife, and several of them (Manu, the Talmud, the Pali canon) specify the heavenly destination with the same concreteness Valluvar does.

tamil:
புகழ்புரிந்த இல்லிலோர்க்கு இல்லை இகழ்வார்முன்
ஏறுபோல் பீடு நடை.
transliteration:
Pugazhpurindha illiloarkku illai igazhvaarmun,
ERupoal peedu nadai.
current_meaning: A man whose wife does not care for the household's good name cannot walk with the proud, lion-like stride before those who hold him in contempt.
elementary_explanation: Imagine walking into a room where people are whispering about you. If you know you've done nothing wrong at home, you can walk in with your head up. If you know you have, your feet get heavy. This kural says a family's good name is what lets someone stand tall in front of people who don't like them.
university_explanation: Valluvar shifts register here from the household's interior to its public face, and the image he chooses — ERu, the bull or male lion, with peedu nadai, a gait of dignified swagger — is drawn from the heroic vocabulary of Sangam puRam poetry, where such a walk signals a warrior's untouchable standing. Parimelazhagar reads the couplet as stating the specific defect that follows when the soR-kaappu of Kural 56 is neglected, which makes 55–59 a tightly argued sequence rather than a list. The sociology behind it is worth naming: in the honour economy of ancient Tamil society, a household's puhaz was a collective asset that any member could deplete, so Valluvar's claim is descriptive as much as normative — the man's public bearing is materially constituted by his wife's reputation. Modern readers rightly note the asymmetry (the wife's conduct determines the husband's honour, but the couplet says nothing of the reverse) and the fact that this logic is precisely what later hardened into honour-based control of women; it is worth setting beside Kural 57, where Valluvar explicitly rejects control as a method. Comparative wisdom literature converges here almost uncannily: Proverbs 31:23, Bava Metzia 59a, and Odyssey 11 all tie a man's standing in the public assembly directly to his wife.

tamil:
மங்கலம் என்ப மனைமாட்சி மற்று அதன்
நன்கலம் நன்மக்கட் பேறு.
transliteration:
Mangalam enba manaimaatchi matru adhan,
nankalam nanmakkat peRu.
current_meaning: The wise say that the wife's excellence is the true auspiciousness of a home; and that good children are the fine jewel with which that auspiciousness is adorned.
elementary_explanation: A birthday cake is the good part. The candles on top make it look even better — but they're not the cake. This kural says the wife's goodness is the cake and good children are the candles: lovely, but only because there's something underneath to put them on.
university_explanation: The couplet closes the chapter on a two-term metaphor of extraordinary economy: manaimaatchi is mangalam (the auspicious thing itself, the blessing), and children are its nan-kalam (its good ornament) — and the near-pun between mangalam and nankalam binds the two halves phonetically while separating them logically. The hierarchy matters: an ornament presupposes something to adorn, so Valluvar is explicitly subordinating progeny to character, a striking priority in a culture where sons carried ritual obligations for the ancestors. Parimelazhagar supplies the unstated subject — enba, 'so the knowing say' — and observes that the couplet functions as a thoRRuvaay, a doorway opening onto Chapter 7 (Makkat-peRu), so that the chapter's last word is also the next chapter's first subject. The comparative field here is unusually convergent, since almost every tradition pairs a virtuous wife with flourishing children as a single image of blessing: Psalm 128 does it with a vine and olive shoots, the Qur'an with 'comfort of the eyes', and the Pali Maṅgala Sutta — which shares the very word maṅgala with the Tamil mangalam through their common Indic root — lists care for partner and children among the highest blessings.

tamil:
பெறுமவற்றுள் யாமறிவது இல்லை அறிவறிந்த
மக்கட்பேறு அல்ல பிற.
transliteration:
Perumavatrul Yaamarivadhu Illai Arivarindha,
Makkatperu Alla Pira.
current_meaning: Among all the good things a person may come to possess, we know of none greater than having children who have learned what is worth knowing.
elementary_explanation: Imagine someone gives you a huge pile of presents — toys, money, a big house. This kural says that if you also had a child who grows up kind and clever, that child would be the best present of all, better than everything else in the pile put together.
university_explanation: Valluvar opens the chapter on progeny by ranking it above every other பேறு (pēṟu, "gain, acquisition") a householder can obtain, and the qualifier is decisive: not merely மக்கட்பேறு (makkaṭ-pēṟu, the getting of children) but அறிவறிந்த மக்கட்பேறு — children who have "known what is to be known." The reduplicative phrase அறிவு அறிந்த is characteristically Kural-like compression: it makes discernment, not mere biological succession, the thing being praised. Parimēlaḻakar, the fourteenth-century commentator, frames the whole adhikāram through the pan-Indic doctrine of the three debts (ṛṇa-traya) owed by the twice-born — to the sages, discharged by study; to the gods, by sacrifice; and to the ancestors (தென்புலத்தார், ten-pulattār), discharged only by begetting offspring — which is why the chapter follows immediately on marriage and the worth of a wife. Notably, Valluvar himself never invokes that ritual apparatus: he argues purely from the sweetness and social worth of the thing itself, which is part of why the text reads as equally at home in Jain, Śaiva and secular frameworks. The use of the first-person plural யாம் ("we know of none") is also worth marking — it is the voice of considered human judgement rather than revelation.

tamil:
எழுபிறப்பும் தீயவை தீண்டா பழிபிறங்காப்
பண்புடை மக்கட் பெறின்.
transliteration:
Ezhupirappum Theeyavai Theendaa Pazhipirangaap,
Panbudai Makkat Perin.
current_meaning: If one begets children of good character, against whom no reproach can be raised, then through all seven births no evil will come near.
elementary_explanation: Think of a family like a long relay race, with each generation passing the baton on. This kural says that if you raise children who do good and never give anyone a reason to blame them, the whole race stays clean — trouble never catches up with your family, not for a very, very long time.
university_explanation: The phrase எழுபிறப்பு (ezhu-piṟappu, "seven births") invokes the classical Indian reckoning of the sevenfold cycle of embodied existence, and Parimēlaḻakar's gloss here is explicitly transmigrational: the parent's accumulated evil karma is worn away by the meritorious acts a virtuous child performs on their behalf. The key qualifier is பழிபிறங்காப் பண்புடை — character (paṇpu) so ordered that பழி (paḻi, public blame or reproach) never rises around it. Valluvar thus binds an other-worldly promise to an entirely this-worldly test: the proof of the child's virtue is that no one can speak ill of them. Whether "seven births" is read literally as rebirths (the Jain and Hindu reading) or idiomatically as "seven generations" — which is how the modern commentator M. Karunanidhi renders it — the structural claim is the same: a child's good conduct is retroactively protective of those who produced them. That inversion of the usual direction of moral influence, from child upward to parent, is what makes the couplet distinctive.

tamil:
தம்பொருள் என்பதம் மக்கள் அவர்பொருள்
தம்தம் வினையான் வரும்.
transliteration:
Thamporul Enpadham Makkal Avarporul,
Thamdham Vinaiyaan Varum.
current_meaning: The wise say that one's children are one's true wealth; and whatever wealth those children come to have arrives through the deeds each of them performs.
elementary_explanation: Grown-ups sometimes call money their "treasure." This kural says the real treasure is your children. And here's the second part: nobody can just hand a child a good life the way you hand over a coin — what each child ends up with comes from the things they themselves do.
university_explanation: The couplet turns on a deliberate double use of பொருள் (poruḷ, "wealth, substance, thing of worth"): children are the parents' poruḷ, and the children in turn have a poruḷ of their own, which arrives by வினை (viṉai, "deed, act, karma"). Parimēlaḻakar reads the second line as meaning that the good deeds children perform on their parents' behalf return to the parents as wealth; Maṇakkuṭavar and several moderns read it more directly, that each person's fortune follows from their own acts. Valluvar's compression permits both, and the ambiguity is productive: the family is a genuine economy of worth, yet no share in it is transferable by mere inheritance. The phrase தம்தம் ("each one's own") is the load-bearing word — it individuates moral responsibility inside a verse that has just made the family a single unit of value. That tension between collective wealth and non-transferable desert is what makes this the philosophically sharpest couplet in the chapter, and it anticipates the Kural's later chapter on ஊழ் (Fate).

tamil:
அமிழ்தினும் ஆற்ற இனிதேதம் மக்கள்
சிறுகை அளாவிய கூழ்.
transliteration:
Amizhdhinum Aatra Inidhedham Makkal,
Sirukai Alaaviya Koozh.
current_meaning: Far sweeter than the nectar of the gods is plain boiled food that one's own children have stirred about with their little hands.
elementary_explanation: Imagine the most delicious dessert in the world — the kind a king would eat. Now imagine ordinary rice that your little brother or sister has squished and messed up with their tiny fingers. This kural says the messy rice tastes better. Not because of the rice — because of whose hands were in it.
university_explanation: This is perhaps the most quoted couplet in the Kural's domestic chapters, and its power lies in a calculated collision of registers. அமிழ்து (amiḻtu, Sanskrit amṛta) is the immortalising nectar of the gods, the top of the classical scale of sweetness; கூழ் (kūḻ) is at the bottom — a thin boiled gruel or mash, the plainest food in the Tamil larder. Between them Valluvar inserts the word that does all the work: அளாவிய (aḷāviya), "stirred, mixed about, dabbled in" by a சிறுகை, a "small hand." Parimēlaḻakar glosses அளாவல் by quoting a Puṟanāṉūṟu line about a child "dropping and touching and mouthing and churning" the ghee-rice until it is smeared everywhere — that is, he understands the verse to be describing genuine mess, not a decorous gesture. The theological move is quietly radical: the transcendent standard of sweetness is beaten not by a better food but by a relationship, and the sensory language of the next two couplets (touch, hearing) shows Valluvar building a deliberate small phenomenology of parenthood through the bodily senses.

tamil:
மக்கள்மெய் தீண்டல் உடற்கின்பம் மற்றுஅவர்
சொற்கேட்டல் இன்பம் செவிக்கு.
transliteration:
Makkalmey Theendal Udarkinbam Matravar,
Sorkettal Inbam Sevikku.
current_meaning: To touch the body of one's children is the body's delight; to hear them speak is the ear's delight.
elementary_explanation: Your body has different ways of being happy. Hugging someone you love makes your whole self feel warm — that's happiness for your skin. Listening to someone you love chatter away makes your ears happy. This kural says children give you both at once.
university_explanation: Valluvar constructs the couplet as a strict parallel built on two of the five senses: உடற்கு இன்பம் ("pleasure for the body") paired with செவிக்கு இன்பம் ("pleasure for the ear"), with தீண்டல் (tīṇṭal, touching) answering கேட்டல் (kēṭṭal, hearing). Read against kural 64, which handled taste, the three verses form a deliberate sensory triptych — the chapter argues for the value of children not by doctrine but by cataloguing the specific bodily goods they confer. Parimēlaḻakar makes an interesting interpretive choice here: he notes that Valluvar writes simply சொல் ("speech") rather than the மழலைச்சொல் ("lisping speech") of the following couplet, and concludes that the verse covers not only infant babble but the learned speech of grown children as well, so that the ear's pleasure lasts a lifetime. The grammatical abstract nouns தீண்டல் and கேட்டல் are, in his reading, standing by metonymy for the acts themselves — a small point of Tamil grammatical commentary that shows how closely this tradition read the couplets.

tamil:
குழல்இனிது யாழ்இனிது என்பதம் மக்கள்
மழலைச்சொல் கேளா தவர்.
transliteration:
Kuzhalinidhu Yaazhinidhu Enpadham Makkal,
Mazhalaichchol Kelaadhavar.
current_meaning: "The flute is sweet, the lute is sweet" — so say only those who have never heard the lisping speech of their own children.
elementary_explanation: Some people say the most beautiful sound in the world is music. This kural teases them a little: they only think that because they have never sat and listened to a toddler talking nonsense. If they had, they would know which sound really wins.
university_explanation: The couplet is the Kural's most famous piece of wit, and its structure is a rhetorical trap. Valluvar never asserts that a child's babble is sweeter than music; he simply reports who it is that ranks music first — namely, those who have not heard மழலைச்சொல் (maḻalai-c-col), the half-formed lisping speech of a small child. Parimēlaḻakar identifies the remainder as a குறிப்பெச்சம், a deliberately unspoken implication that the reader is left to supply, and Maṇakkuṭavar makes it blunt: "those who have heard do not say it." The two instruments named are not decorative: the குழல் (kuḻal, the transverse flute) and the யாழ் (yāḻ, the ancient Tamil harp-lute) were the paired standards of vocal-and-instrumental excellence in the Caṅkam musical system, so Valluvar is measuring the child's voice against the recognised summit of the art. The word maḻalai has since passed into ordinary Tamil as an affectionate term for toddler-speech largely on the strength of this verse.

tamil:
தந்தை மகற்காற்றும் நன்றி அவையத்து
முந்தி இருப்பச் செயல்.
transliteration:
Thandhai Makarkaatrum Nandri Avaiyaththu,
Mundhi Iruppach Cheyal.
current_meaning: The good that a father owes his son is to make him fit to sit in the front rank of the assembly of the learned.
elementary_explanation: A dad can give his child lots of things — toys, money, a bike. This kural says the best gift is different: teach your child so well that when clever grown-ups sit down to talk, your child is the one they want sitting at the front.
university_explanation: The couplet defines the father's duty with unusual precision. நன்றி (naṉṟi) here means the benefit or good office a father performs, and the content of that benefit is not property but standing: to be able to sit முந்தி (muntī, "foremost, ahead") in the அவை (avai), the learned assembly. The avai was a real institution in the Tamil and broader Indic world — the court or scholarly council where reputation was won by demonstrated learning and skill in speech — and the Kural devotes two later chapters, அவையறிதல் and அவையஞ்சாமை, to how one conducts oneself there. Parimēlaḻakar draws the sharpest possible conclusion from the wording: making a son wealthy, he says, cannot count as நன்றி at all, because wealth brings suffering; only education does. The couplet thus quietly converts the entire chapter's language of "wealth" into a claim about cultural capital, and it is this verse, with 68, that makes Chapter 7 one of the most-cited passages in modern Tamil arguments for universal education.

tamil:
தம்மின்தம் மக்கள் அறிவுடைமை மாநிலத்து
மன்னுயிர்க் கெல்லாம் இனிது.
transliteration:
Thammindham Makkal Arivudaimai Maanilaththu,
Mannuyirk Kellaam Inidhu.
current_meaning: That one's children should be wiser than oneself is sweet not only to the parents but to every living being on this great earth.
elementary_explanation: When you get better at something than your teacher or your parents, nobody minds — everyone is delighted. This kural says that is one of the few kinds of being-beaten that makes the whole world happy.
university_explanation: The compressed opening தம்மின்தம் மக்கள் அறிவுடைமை carries an ambiguity the commentators split over. Parimēlaḻakar reads தம்மின் as "more than to themselves" — the children's wisdom is sweeter to all the world's beings than it is even to the parents — and takes மன்னுயிர் ("enduring lives") to stand specifically for the discerning, since only they can appreciate learning. Most moderns, including M. Varadarajan and Karunanidhi, read தம்மின் comparatively of the children instead: that the children surpass the parents in wisdom. Either way, the verse performs a striking widening of scope. Having spent four couplets on the private senses — taste, touch, hearing — Valluvar suddenly extends the circle to மாநிலத்து மன்னுயிர்க்கெல்லாம், every living thing on the great earth. The claim is that a child's intelligence is a non-rival public good: unlike wealth or rank, one family's gain in wisdom costs no one anything and delights everyone. That move, from the household to the biosphere in a single line, is characteristic of the Kural's method throughout the household chapters.

tamil:
ஈன்ற பொழுதின் பெரிதுவக்கும் தன்மகனைச்
சான்றோன் எனக்கேட்ட தாய்.
transliteration:
Eendra Pozhudhin Peridhuvakkum Thanmakanaich,
Chaandron Enakketta Thaai.
current_meaning: A mother who hears her son spoken of as a person of true worth rejoices more in that moment than she did in the hour she gave birth to him.
elementary_explanation: The day a baby is born is one of the happiest days a mother ever has. But this kural says there is a day that beats it: the day she overhears other people saying her child has grown up to be a genuinely good person.
university_explanation: The couplet's force comes from the word சான்றோன் (cāṉṟōṉ), from the root சால் — "filled up, complete, sufficient." A cāṉṟōṉ is not merely a clever or successful man but one who is full in character, and the term carries enormous weight in Tamil ethical vocabulary; the Kural devotes a whole later chapter, சான்றாண்மை, to the quality. The second load-bearing word is கேட்ட (kēṭṭa, "having heard"): the mother's supreme joy arrives not from seeing but from hearing others say it. Parimēlaḻakar reads this carefully, arguing that the ordinary joy of birth is the joy of what is seen with the eyes on one's lap, while this is the distinct and greater joy of hearing one's child pronounced complete by those qualified to judge. He also notes that the couplet names the mother specifically because her joy admits of no measure, which is why Valluvar separates it from the father's case in 67. Read alongside 70, the chapter closes with a matched pair — the mother's joy, then the father's requital — with public reputation as the currency of both.

tamil:
மகன்தந்தைக்கு ஆற்றும் உதவி இவன்தந்தை
என்நோற்றான் கொல்எனும் சொல்.
transliteration:
Makandhandhaikku Aatrum Udhavi Ivandhandhai,
Ennotraan Kol Enum Sol.
current_meaning: The service a son renders his father is to live so that people say, "What austerities must this man's father have performed, to deserve such a son?"
elementary_explanation: How does a child pay a parent back? Not with money. This kural says you pay them back by being so good that when people meet you they think, "Wow — whoever raised this person must have done something really special."
university_explanation: The chapter closes by completing the reciprocal pair begun in 67: there the father's duty was to place the son foremost in the assembly; here the son's உதவி (utavi, "help, requital") is to generate a particular sentence in other people's mouths. The verb நோல் / நோற்றல் (nōṟṟal) means to undertake tapas — ascetic austerity, penance — so என்நோற்றான் கொல் literally asks "what penance can he have performed?" The idiom presumes the karmic economy in which a son of high quality is earned by merit, and Valluvar's wit is to make the son's whole filial duty consist in causing that inference to be drawn. Parimēlaḻakar underlines the point that the requital is owed specifically to the father who made him learned — i.e. it answers couplet 67 directly — and he glosses சொல் as standing, by metonymy, for the conduct that produces the saying. Note what the couplet conspicuously does not say: nothing about supporting parents in old age, obedience, or ritual duty. The entire obligation is discharged through character as publicly perceived, which is a strikingly reputational, non-transactional construal of filial piety.

tamil:
அன்பிற்கும் உண்டோ அடைக்குந்தாழ் ஆர்வலர்
புன்கணீர் பூசல் தரும்.
transliteration:
Anbirkum undo adaikkundhaazh aarvalar,
Punkaneer poosal tharum.
current_meaning: Is there any bolt that can lock love up inside? The small tears that fall from a loving person's eyes when someone dear is suffering will publish that hidden love to the whole world.
elementary_explanation: Imagine trying to keep a puppy shut inside a box — it will still wiggle and whine and everyone will know it's there. Love is like that. Even if you never say "I love you," the moment someone you care about gets hurt, your eyes fill up and everybody can see exactly how you feel.
university_explanation: Valluvar opens the chapter on அன்பு (anbu, love) with an argument from evidence rather than exhortation. தாழ் (thaazh) is the wooden bolt or latch of a door, and the rhetorical question அடைக்குந்தாழ் உண்டோ — "is there a latch that shuts it in?" — treats love as a physical presence that leaks past every attempt at concealment. The proof offered is deliberately small: புன்கணீர் (punkaneer), literally "mean" or "slight" eye-water, a single involuntary tear shed for an ஆர்வலர் (aarvalar, one who is loved/desired). The commentator Parimelalhagar notes that love may not be available to காட்சி அளவை (perception) directly, yet it is established by அனுமான அளவை (inference) — a striking use of the technical vocabulary of Indian epistemology to argue that inner states are publicly readable through their effects. பூசல் (poosal) means a public outcry or uproar, so the couplet's paradox is that the quietest possible sign makes the loudest possible announcement.

tamil:
அன்பிலார் எல்லாம் தமக்குரியர் அன்புடையார்
என்பும் உரியர் பிறர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Anbilaar ellaam thamakkuriyar anbudaiyaar,
Enbum uriyar pirarkku.
current_meaning: People without love claim everything as their own; people who have love regard even their own bones as belonging to others.
elementary_explanation: Think about two kids with a bag of sweets. One says, "These are mine, nobody touch them." The other hands them around until the bag is empty, and is happier for it. This kural says a loving person gives so completely that they would give away their very bones if it helped someone else.
university_explanation: The couplet is built on a sharp antithesis of possession: எல்லாம் தமக்கு உரியர் ("all things belong to them") versus என்பும் உரியர் பிறர்க்கு ("even bones belong to others"). The word உரிமை/உரியர் is a legal term of ownership, so Valluvar is deliberately using the vocabulary of property law to describe self-giving. என்பு (enbu, bone) is the harshest, least giveable part of the body — the opposite of the money or grain one might expect a charity verse to mention — and its choice pushes generosity past the limit of comfort. Note also the chapter's internal sound-play: அன்பு (love) and என்பு (bone) are near-rhymes that Valluvar will exploit again in Kurals 73, 77 and 80, binding the ethical argument to the anatomy of the body. Many commentators, including Manakkudavar and Parimelalhagar, read the second line as covering not only the corpse but the whole living self placed at the disposal of others.

tamil:
அன்போடு இயைந்த வழக்கென்ப ஆருயிர்க்கு
என்போடு இயைந்த தொடர்பு.
transliteration:
Anbodu iyaindha vazhakkenba aaruyirkku,
Enbodu iyaindha thodarbu.
current_meaning: The wise say that the precious life's union with a body of flesh and bone exists for the sake of a life lived in union with love — love is the reason the soul is embodied at all.
elementary_explanation: Why do you have a body at all — arms, hands, a voice? This kural says: so that you can love people with them. A hug needs arms. Helping needs hands. The body is the tool love uses, and that is what it is for.
university_explanation: This is the philosophical hinge of the chapter. The couplet pairs two uses of இயைந்த (iyaindha, "joined with"): the soul's joining with என்பு (bone/body) and the life's joining with அன்பு (love), and asserts that the first exists as the வழக்கு — the settled practice, warrant, or rationale — of the second. ஆருயிர் (aaruyir, "rare/precious life") marks the soul as something hard-won, which sharpens the question of what it is embodied for. Parimelalhagar and later commentators read the verse causally, with some giving it a karmic gloss (embodiment as the fruit of love practised in a former birth) and others, including modern readers like M. Varadarajan, reading it teleologically: bodily existence is *for* loving. Either way Valluvar refuses a view in which the body is a mere prison for the soul — a pointed position in a South Asian intellectual landscape crowded with world-renouncing ascetic schools — and instead makes embodied relationship the point of having been born.

tamil:
அன்புஈனும் ஆர்வம் உடைமை அதுஈனும்
நண்பு என்னும் நாடாச் சிறப்பு.
transliteration:
Anbu eenum aarvam udaimai adhu eenum,
Nanbu ennum naadaach chirappu.
current_meaning: Love gives birth to warm eagerness toward others, and that eagerness in turn gives birth to friendship — an excellence so great that it exceeds anything one could go looking for.
elementary_explanation: Love works like a seed that grows into a plant that makes more seeds. First you care about somebody. Then you want to be around them and do things for them. Then, before you notice, you have a friend — and friendship is one of the best things anyone can have.
university_explanation: The couplet is constructed as a genealogy, with ஈனும் (eenum, "begets, gives birth to") repeated to stage a two-step generation: அன்பு → ஆர்வம் → நண்பு. ஆர்வம் (aarvam) is warm eagerness or attentive desire toward another — the same root that gave ஆர்வலர் in Kural 71 — and Valluvar places it as the middle term that converts a disposition into a relationship. The closing phrase நாடாச் சிறப்பு is the verse's most striking move: நாடா means "unsought" or "not to be searched out," so friendship is an excellence that cannot be acquired by pursuit and arrives only as the by-product of love already given. This anticipates the entire நட்பியல் (the book of friendship, chapters 79–87) in the Poruṭpāl, and it separates Valluvar from purely transactional accounts of alliance: friendship here is emergent, not negotiated.

tamil:
அன்புற்று அமர்ந்த வழக்கென்ப வையகத்து
இன்புற்றார் எய்தும் சிறப்பு.
transliteration:
Anbutru amarndha vazhakkenba vaiyagaththu,
Inbutraar eydhum sirappu.
current_meaning: The distinction enjoyed by those who live happily in this world is, the wise say, simply the fruit of a life settled in love.
elementary_explanation: Have you ever noticed that the happiest people you know are usually the ones with the most love around them — not the ones with the most stuff? This kural says that is not a coincidence. The good life people admire grows out of loving.
university_explanation: Kural 75 reuses the frame of Kural 73 — வழக்கென்ப, "the wise call it the natural practice/consequence of" — but shifts the payoff from metaphysics to lived happiness. The key verb is அமர்ந்த (amarndha), "settled, seated, at rest in": love here is not a passing rush of feeling but a stable condition one dwells in. சிறப்பு (sirappu) denotes honour, distinction, the visible excellence others recognise in a life. Crucially Valluvar locates this reward வையகத்து, "in this world," not in a heaven — a consistent feature of his ethics, which repeatedly argues that virtue pays here and now in the ordinary domestic register of the இல்லறவியல் (the book of household life). The couplet therefore functions as a rebuttal of the assumption that the loving must sacrifice their own happiness: for Valluvar, love is not the price of a good life but its mechanism.

tamil:
அறத்திற்கே அன்புசார் பென்ப அறியார்
மறத்திற்கும் அஃதே துணை.
transliteration:
Araththirke anbusaar benba ariyaar,
Maraththirkum aqdhe thunai.
current_meaning: Only the ignorant say that love is the support of virtue alone; love is just as much the support of forceful, martial action.
elementary_explanation: People think being loving means being soft. But think of a mother bird when something comes near her nest — she will fight anything. The same love that makes you gentle is what makes you brave when someone you love is in danger.
university_explanation: This is the most counter-intuitive couplet in the chapter and the one most argued over by commentators. The pair அறம் / மறம் (aram / maram) is a classical Tamil opposition: aram is righteousness and dharma, while maram is martial valour, ferocity, the warrior's fighting spirit (the word also shades toward "wrath" or "cruelty"). Valluvar's claim is that அன்பு is the துணை — the support, companion, aid — of both. Parimelalhagar reads maram narrowly, as the legitimate severity with which a ruler punishes wrongdoing; modern commentators such as Karunanidhi read it broadly as வீரம், heroism. Either way the verse blocks a sentimental reading of the whole chapter: love in the Kural is not synonymous with mildness, and Valluvar will later devote whole chapters to armies, kingship and punishment without contradiction. The underlying logic is that ferocity in defence of what one loves is itself a form of love, not its abandonment.

tamil:
என்பி லதனை வெயில்போலக் காயுமே
அன்பி லதனை அறம்.
transliteration:
Enbi ladhanai veyilpolak kaayume,
Anbi ladhanai aram.
current_meaning: Just as the blazing sun scorches the boneless creature that creeps in the open, so righteousness itself scorches the life that has no love in it.
elementary_explanation: Have you ever seen a worm caught on hot pavement in the sun? It has no shell and no bones, so it shrivels fast. This kural says a person with no love in them is just as unprotected — goodness itself will feel unbearable to them.
university_explanation: The couplet works by a tight phonetic parallel: என்பு இலதனை ("the boneless one") and அன்பு இலதனை ("the loveless one") differ by a single vowel, so the analogy is carried in the sound before the sense arrives. The traditional referent of என்பிலது is the earthworm or grub, a creature with no skeleton, which the Tamil commentators from Manakkudavar onward identify explicitly (புழு, worm). The force of the verse lies in its reversal of expectation: அறம் (aram, righteousness/dharma) is normally the protector, but here it is the destroyer — not because it attacks, but because the loveless creature has no internal structure with which to withstand it. Valluvar is claiming that love is to moral life what bone is to a body: the load-bearing frame. Without it, exposure to the moral order is simply lethal. This also sets up Kurals 79 and 80, which make the anatomical metaphor explicit.

tamil:
அன்பகத் தில்லா உயிர்வாழ்க்கை வன்பாற்கண்
வற்றல் மரந்தளிர்த் தற்று.
transliteration:
Anbagath thillaa uyirvaazhkkai vanbaarkan,
Vatral marandhalirth thatru.
current_meaning: A life lived without love in the heart is like a dead, dried-up tree putting out green shoots in a barren desert — an appearance of flourishing with nothing real behind it.
elementary_explanation: Picture a dry stick standing in hot sand suddenly growing green leaves. It could not really happen, and if it looked like it did, something would be wrong. This kural says a life with no love in it is like that: it might look like it is going fine, but it is not really alive.
university_explanation: The comparison is doubly impossible and that is the point. வற்றல் மரம் is a tree already dried dead, and வன்பாற்கண் is the வன்புலம் or hard, waterless tract — the பாலை landscape of classical Tamil poetics, the desert region associated in akam convention with separation and deprivation. A dead tree sprouting in the desert is not merely unlikely; the couplet's force is that it is a contradiction dressed as a phenomenon. Valluvar is not saying the loveless life is unhappy — he is saying it is not life (உயிர்வாழ்க்கை) at all, only its outward semblance. The use of the tiṇai landscape vocabulary quietly imports the whole emotional register of பாலை (barrenness, loss, the unwatered heart) into an ethical argument, a characteristic Valluvar move of compressing a poetic tradition into seven words.

tamil:
புறத்துறுப் பெல்லாம் எவன்செய்யும் யாக்கை
அகத்துறுப்பு அன்பி லவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Puraththurup pellaam evanseyyum yaakkai,
Agaththuruppu anbi lavarkku.
current_meaning: What use are all the outward limbs and organs to those who lack love, which is the body's inner organ?
elementary_explanation: A guitar can have perfect strings, shiny wood and beautiful tuning pegs — but if there's no hollow space inside it, it makes no music. This kural says love is the inside part of a person. Without it, all the outside parts don't accomplish anything.
university_explanation: Valluvar builds the couplet on a precise anatomical contrast: புறத்து உறுப்பு (external organ/limb) against அகத்து உறுப்பு (internal organ), and then makes the startling classificatory claim that அன்பு is itself an உறுப்பு — a bodily organ, not a sentiment. யாக்கை (yaakkai) is the physical frame or corporeal body. The rhetorical question எவன் செய்யும் ("what will they accomplish?") is not asking whether the limbs are pleasant but whether they can function at all, on the analogy of a body whose vital inner organ has failed. Commentators split on the referent: Parimelalhagar and Solomon Pappaiah extend it to the "external organs" of a household — its wealth, servants and property — arguing that a home without love is equally inoperative, while Varadarajan and Karunanidhi keep it to the individual body. Both readings converge on the same deflationary verdict about outward equipment, and the verse reads as a direct ancestor of the argument in Kural 80.

tamil:
அன்பின் வழியது உயிர்நிலை அஃதிலார்க்கு
என்புதோல் போர்த்த உடம்பு.
transliteration:
Anbin vazhiyadhu uyirnilai aqdhilaarkku,
Enbudhol porththa udambu.
current_meaning: A body that moves along the path of love is what it means to be truly alive; for those without love, the body is nothing but bones wrapped in a covering of skin.
elementary_explanation: A house with people laughing and cooking inside is a home. The same house with nobody in it is just walls. This kural says a person without love is like that empty house — everything is still standing, but nobody is living there.
university_explanation: The chapter closes by pushing its anatomical argument to its conclusion. உயிர்நிலை (uyir-nilai) means the "state" or "seat" of life — the condition in which a body actually counts as living — and Valluvar makes that condition dependent on அன்பின் வழி, the path or way of love. The second line's என்பு தோல் போர்த்த உடம்பு is deliberately clinical: bone with skin stretched over it, the description of a cadaver or a scarecrow, and it completes the அன்பு/என்பு wordplay that has run through Kurals 72, 73 and 77. The couplet is frequently cited as the single most quoted line of the chapter and has become proverbial in Tamil. Philosophically it takes a definite position in a live ancient debate about what individuates a living being: Valluvar's answer is neither breath nor consciousness but relationship. A body that does not move along love's path may be biologically intact and is nonetheless, by his definition, not the seat of a life.

tamil:
இருந்தோம்பி இல்வாழ்வ தெல்லாம் விருந்தோம்பி
வேளாண்மை செய்தற் பொருட்டு.
transliteration:
Irundhombi ilvaazhva thellaam virundhombi,
Velaanmai seydhar poruttu.
current_meaning: The whole business of settling down, guarding a home and its goods, and living the householder's life exists for one purpose: to cherish guests and render them generous service.
elementary_explanation: Why does a family have a house, a kitchen and food in the cupboard? This kural says it isn't just so the family can eat. It's so that when someone knocks on the door — a traveller, a neighbour, someone hungry — there is something ready to share. The house is like a well: it holds water so that whoever is thirsty can drink.
university_explanation: Valluvar opens the chapter on hospitality with a startling inversion of economic logic: the entire apparatus of the household — இருத்தல் (settling/dwelling), ஓம்புதல் (guarding, tending, husbanding resources) — is declared instrumental to விருந்தோம்பல், the cherishing of guests. The key term வேளாண்மை (vēḷāṇmai) is untranslatable in one word: it carries the sense of 'husbandry' and of unrepayable benevolence rendered without expectation, and Valluvar reuses it at Kural 212 for the purpose of earned wealth generally. Parimelalagar's classical commentary sharpens the point by contrasting the householder with the forest renunciant: one stays in the house precisely in order to have something to give, so that if no benevolence is done, the toil of acquisition has no fruit at all. This makes hospitality not a courtesy appended to domestic life but its justifying cause — a claim structurally parallel to the Sanskrit doctrine that the household exists to sustain the other three āśramas, yet arrived at here without any appeal to caste, ritual, or scripture.

tamil:
விருந்து புறத்ததாத் தானுண்டல் சாவா
மருந்தெனினும் வேண்டற்பாற் றன்று.
transliteration:
Virundhu puraththadhaath thaanundal saavaa,
Marundhu eninum vendarpaatru andru.
current_meaning: To eat by yourself while a guest is left standing outside is not a thing worth wanting — not even if what is on your plate were the medicine that abolishes death.
elementary_explanation: Imagine you were handed a magic sweet that would let you live forever. But your friend is waiting outside the door, hungry, and you shut the door and eat it alone. This kural says: then the magic sweet isn't worth having. What you eat matters far less than who you eat it with.
university_explanation: Valluvar builds the verse on a deliberately extreme hypothetical: சாவா மருந்து, the 'deathless medicine' (the amṛta of pan-Indian myth, the elixir gods themselves fight over). The rhetorical structure is a fortiori — if even immortality is not worth eating alone, then plainly nothing else is. புறத்ததா ('being outside') is doing precise ethical work: the fault is not refusing the guest outright but the far commoner domestic evasion of simply not noticing that someone is out there. Manakkudavar's tenth-century gloss defines the whole chapter as the rule that 'when strangers arrive at mealtime, one must divide and eat,' locating hospitality at the specific moment of consumption. The verse belongs to a widespread ancient horror of solitary eating, found equally in the Vedic yajña-remnant doctrine and in Greek sympotic ethics, but Valluvar states it with unusual economy: the guest's presence, not the food's value, determines whether a meal is worth taking.

tamil:
வருவிருந்து வைகலும் ஓம்புவான் வாழ்க்கை
பருவந்து பாழ்படுதல் இன்று.
transliteration:
Varuvirundhu vaigalum ombuvaan vaazhkkai,
Paruvandhu paazhpadudhal indru.
current_meaning: The household of one who tends arriving guests day after day will never be worn down into ruin by doing so.
elementary_explanation: People sometimes worry: if I keep giving food away to visitors, won't I run out? This kural says no — like a well that keeps filling back up the more you draw from it, a home that keeps feeding guests doesn't dry up. Giving every day doesn't empty the house.
university_explanation: Having established the duty, Valluvar now answers the obvious objection: won't constant hospitality bankrupt you? The reply hinges on two compact words — பருவந்து (suffering hardship, being worn down) and பாழ்படுதல் (falling into waste, ruin). வைகலும் ('every day') is essential: the claim is specifically about habitual, repeated hospitality, not a single grand feast. Mu. Varadarajan's modern commentary reads the verse as a promise that such a life will never be ruined 'on account of that' — the causal clause matters, since Valluvar is not promising immunity from all misfortune but denying that hospitality is the cause of any. This is characteristic of the Kural's ethical naturalism: rather than invoking divine reward, it states a claim about how generous households actually fare, one echoed in the near-universal folk motif of the vessel that never empties.

tamil:
அகனமர்ந்து செய்யாள் உறையும் முகனமர்ந்து
நல்விருந்து ஓம்புவான் இல்.
transliteration:
Aganamarndhu seyyaal uraiyum muganamarndhu,
Nalvirundhu ombuvaan il.
current_meaning: In the house of the man who welcomes worthy guests with a glad face, Fortune herself settles down and makes her home, gladly.
elementary_explanation: Good luck is pictured here as a guest too — and she only stays where she feels welcome. If you greet visitors with a warm, happy face, Fortune decides she likes it in your house and moves in. A frown at the door sends her away again.
university_explanation: The verse turns on a deliberate mirroring: அகன் அமர்ந்து ('settling gladly within') describes the goddess, while முகன் அமர்ந்து ('gladdening the face') describes the host — the same verb அமர் binds the host's countenance to the deity's contentment. செய்யாள், 'the red one,' is the Tamil epithet for Lakshmi/Śrī, the goddess of prosperity, invoked here not as an object of worship but as a personified consequence. Crucially, Valluvar specifies நல்விருந்து, the *good* guest, introducing discrimination into hospitality that the chapter elsewhere leaves open. The verse also quietly introduces the chapter's second great theme, which will dominate Kural 90: that the host's face, not the host's larder, is the operative instrument of hospitality. It is one of the few places in the Aṟattuppāl where Valluvar permits himself a mythological figure, and even here Śrī functions less as a deity than as a way of saying that wealth behaves like a guest and stays where it is well received.

tamil:
வித்தும் இடல்வேண்டும் கொல்லோ விருந்தோம்பி
மிச்சில் மிசைவான் புலம்.
transliteration:
Viththum idal vendum kollo virundhombi,
Michchil misaivaan pulam.
current_meaning: Does the field of the man who feeds his guests first and eats only what is left over even need to be sown?
elementary_explanation: Think of someone who always lets visitors eat first and takes the leftovers for himself. This kural asks, with a smile: does his field even need seeds? It's saying his land will be so full of grain that it seems to grow all by itself. Sharing plants a crop you never had to sow.
university_explanation: The verse is a rhetorical question — கொல்லோ is a Tamil particle of wondering interrogation — and its force is hyperbolic rather than agronomic. மிச்சில் ('the remainder, the leftover') is the pivot: the householder who eats the remnant after his guests have eaten is participating in a pan-Indian sacrificial logic in which the leftover of an offering, far from being inferior, is the sanctified portion. Valluvar's innovation is to transpose that logic from the ritual fire to the ordinary dinner and from the priest to the guest. Manakkudavar and later commentators read the question as asserting that such a person's field yields without sowing; modern readers often take it as saying that his generosity is itself the sowing. The agricultural metaphor for giving — seed, field, harvest — is one of the most widely distributed in world religious literature, appearing independently in Vedic, Buddhist, Qur'anic and Pauline texts, and the Kural's compressed version is among the most elegant.

tamil:
செல்விருந்து ஓம்பி வருவிருந்து பார்த்திருப்பான்
நல்வருந்து வானத் தவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Selvirundhu ombi varuvirundhu paarththiruppaan,
Nalvarundhu vaanath thavarkku.
current_meaning: The man who has cared for the guest now departing and sits watching the road for the guest still to come is himself a welcome guest to those who dwell in heaven.
elementary_explanation: Some people are glad when the visitors finally leave. This kural describes the opposite kind of person: he waves one guest off and then sits by the door looking down the road, hoping someone else will come. That person, it says, is exactly the kind of visitor heaven would love to have.
university_explanation: The verse is built on a triple play with விருந்து: செல்விருந்து (the departing guest), வருவிருந்து (the arriving guest), and நல்விருந்து (the good guest) — the host, by attending to the first two, becomes the third. Parimelalagar glosses the final phrase as meaning that the man is reborn a deva and becomes a welcome guest among those in heaven, while Manakkudavar adds the sharper practical note that 'watching for the arrival' means not eating at all until a guest is present. The verse thus introduces the chapter's only explicitly eschatological claim, and it does so by an elegant reversal: the perfect host is rewarded not with wealth or honour but by being transformed into the perfect guest. Note that the Tamil here reads நல்வருந்து rather than the expected நல்விருந்து; this is the received reading, attested across the manuscript tradition and reproduced by Parimelalagar, who nonetheless glosses it as நல்விருந்து.

tamil:
இனைத்துணைத் தென்பதொன் றில்லை விருந்தின்
துணைத்துணை வேள்விப் பயன்.
transliteration:
Inaiththunaith thenbadhondru illai virundhin,
Thunaiththunai velvip payan.
current_meaning: There is no fixed amount you can name as the yield of the sacrifice that is hospitality; its measure is the measure of the guest you receive.
elementary_explanation: If you plant a seed, you can roughly guess how much will grow. But this kural says you can't do that with kindness to guests. How much good comes back depends on who walked through your door — and you can never know that in advance, so you should treat everyone well.
university_explanation: Valluvar here names hospitality வேள்வி — sacrifice, the Tamil equivalent of yajña — making explicit what the chapter has implied: feeding a guest is a liturgical act, one of the five great daily sacrifices of the householder, with the guest standing where the fire normally stands. The verse's rhetoric is built on repetition and negation: இனைத்துணைத்து ('of just this much extent') is flatly denied, and replaced by துணைத்துணை ('measure by measure'), a reduplication meaning proportionality without a stated quantity. Parimelalagar defends the claim by quoting Nālaṭiyār 38 — a small gift in worthy hands covers the sky — and concludes that this verse explains why hospitality yields fruit in both this world and the next. The doctrine that merit scales with the recipient's worth is one of the most cross-culturally robust ideas in religious ethics, appearing in nearly identical form in the Pali Abhidhamma, in Jesus's saying about receiving a prophet, and in the Mishnah's list of deeds without measure.

tamil:
பரிந்தோம்பிப் பற்றற்றேம் என்பர் விருந்தோம்பி
வேள்வி தலைப்படா தார்.
transliteration:
Parindhombip patratrem enbar virundhombi,
Velvi thalaippadaa thaar.
current_meaning: Those who never took up the sacrifice of cherishing guests will one day say, with all their anxious hoarding behind them, “We toiled and saved, and now we have nothing to hold on to.”
elementary_explanation: Picture someone who spends their whole life putting food in a locked cupboard and never once shares it. One day they open the cupboard and it's empty, or they're too old to eat it — and they say, sadly, “What was all that for?” This kural says that's what happens when you save everything and give nothing.
university_explanation: The verse is structured as a reported lament: பற்றற்றேம், 'we have become without support/without anything to grasp,' is put directly in the mouths of the failed householders, a rhetorical device Valluvar uses sparingly and to great effect. பரிந்து ('with pain, with anxious care') and ஓம்பி ('guarding') together characterise hoarding as an exhausting labour, quietly contrasting with the same verb ஓம்பி used throughout the chapter for tending guests: the same effort, spent on goods rather than people, ends in destitution. The word வேள்வி again marks hospitality as sacrifice, and தலைப்படாதார் means those who never even embarked on it. The pathos of the verse lies in its temporality — it describes a realisation that arrives too late — placing it in the long tradition of wisdom literature about the rich fool, from Qohelet through the Gospels to the Stoic epistles.

tamil:
உடைமையுள் இன்மை விருந்தோம்பல் ஓம்பா
மடமை மடவார்கண் உண்டு.
transliteration:
Udaimaiyul inmai virundhombal ombaa,
Madamai madavaarkan undu.
current_meaning: Poverty in the midst of plenty is what you get from failing to keep up hospitality — and that particular stupidity is found only in the stupid.
elementary_explanation: Someone can have a full fridge, a big house and lots of money, and still be poor — if they never share any of it. This kural calls that a kind of silliness: having everything and enjoying none of it, because you're too closed-up to let anyone in.
university_explanation: The verse is built on two paradoxes stacked on each other. The first, உடைமையுள் இன்மை ('destitution inside possession'), is a genuine oxymoron and the phrase for which the couplet is best known. The second is the near-tautology of the closing line: மடமை மடவார்கண் உண்டு, 'that folly exists in fools' — a construction that looks empty but functions as a sharp dismissal, refusing to dignify such conduct with any explanation beyond stupidity. மடமை denotes not mere ignorance but a wilful dullness of perception, the inability to see what is obvious. Valluvar thus classifies the inhospitable rich not as wicked but as stupid, a rhetorically devastating move that resurfaces in the Hebrew Bible's treatment of Nabal (whose name is literally 'fool') and in Jesus's address to the rich man as ἄφρων. The couplet completes the chapter's argument: having established hospitality as purpose (81), habit (83), sacrifice (87) and lost opportunity (88), it now names its absence as a form of self-inflicted poverty.

tamil:
மோப்பக் குழையும் அனிச்சம் முகந்திரிந்து
நோக்கக் குழையும் விருந்து.
transliteration:
Moppak kuzhaiyum anichcham mugandhirindhu,
Nokkak kuzhaiyum virundhu.
current_meaning: The anicham flower wilts at the mere act of being smelled; a guest wilts just as fast at a face that turns aside as it looks at him.
elementary_explanation: There's a flower so delicate that it droops the moment you sniff it — you don't even have to touch it. This kural says guests are even more delicate than that. You don't have to say anything unkind; if your face just goes cold when you see them, they wilt.
university_explanation: The chapter closes on its most celebrated image. The அனிச்சம் (anicham) was proverbial in Sangam-era Tamil for extreme delicacy — Valluvar returns to it at Kural 1111 and 1120 in the love poems — and the point of the comparison is a fortiori: the flower at least requires contact with the nostrils, whereas the guest is wilted by nothing more than a look. Parimelalagar's commentary makes the structural argument explicit, listing the three indispensable things a host owes a guest in order: a welcoming face when the guest is still at a distance, kind words as he draws near, and material aid once he is received. Since the face operates first and at a distance, its failure destroys the encounter before hospitality can even begin — which is why Valluvar ends the chapter here rather than with any point about provisions. The couplet is thus the culmination of an argument that has been narrowing steadily from the household's economy (81) to its resources (85) to its liturgy (87) to, finally, a single expression. Note that the received manuscript tradition transmits the second line's verb in a corrupted form in several digital editions; the correct reading, confirmed by Parimelalagar's own gloss, is குழையும், repeating the verb from the first line.

tamil:
இன்சொலால் ஈரம் அளைஇப் படிறுஇலவாம்
செம்பொருள் கண்டார்வாய்ச் சொல்.
transliteration:
Insolaal eeram alaiip padiru ilavaam,
Semporul kandaarvaaich chol.
current_meaning: Truly sweet words are the words that come from the mouths of those who have grasped what is genuinely right — words steeped in warm affection and entirely free of deceit.
elementary_explanation: Kind words are like real honey, not sugar water that only looks sweet. Some people say nice things but are secretly trying to trick you. This kural says real sweet talk has two ingredients: it has to be warm and loving, and it has to be honest. If either one is missing, it isn't the real thing.
university_explanation: Valluvar opens the chapter by defining his terms, a move typical of his method. The Tamil packs three conditions into a single couplet: ஈரம் (eeram, literally 'moistness' — the warmth or tenderness of a heart that is not dry), படிறு இல (padiru ila, 'without guile or fraud'), and செம்பொருள் கண்டார் (semporul kandaar, 'those who have seen the straight/true substance'). Sweet speech is therefore not a rhetorical technique but a moral by-product: it issues from a particular kind of person. This explicitly rules out flattery, the counterfeit that classical ethical traditions across Eurasia were equally anxious to distinguish from genuine kindness — the Tamil padiru occupies almost exactly the space that Greek kolakeia (flattery) and Sanskrit anrta (falsehood in speech) occupy in their respective systems. Placing this definition first also protects the whole remaining chapter from being read as advice on charm or social technique.

tamil:
அகன்அமர்ந்து ஈதலின் நன்றே முகனமர்ந்து
இன்சொலன் ஆகப் பெறின்.
transliteration:
Aganamarndhu eedhalin nandre muganamarndhu,
Insolan aagap perin.
current_meaning: To have a face that lights up and a tongue that speaks kindly is better still than giving a gift with a heart full of goodwill.
elementary_explanation: Imagine two people give you a birthday present. One hands it over without looking up. The other is grinning, says your name, and tells you they hoped you'd like it. The second present feels bigger — even if it cost less. This kural says the warm face and the kind words are worth more than the gift itself.
university_explanation: The couplet sets up a deliberate comparison between two goods that the previous chapters have already praised: ஈதல் (eedhal, giving) and இன்சொல் (insol, sweet speech). Valluvar does not dismiss generosity; he ranks a cheerful countenance and kind word above even generosity offered with an expanded heart (அகன் அமர்ந்து, agan amarndhu — 'the inner self settled in gladness'). The wordplay is structural: அகன் அமர்ந்து (inner gladness) is answered by முகன் அமர்ந்து (mugan amarndhu, 'face settled in gladness'), so the verse argues that the outward, relational expression completes what the inward disposition begins. This ordering — manner above material — is one of the most widely paralleled ideas in world ethical literature, appearing almost verbatim in Ben Sira and in the rabbinic calculus of blessings attached to charity.

tamil:
முகத்தான் அமர்ந்துஇனிது நோக்கி அகத்தானாம்
இன்சொ லினதே அறம்.
transliteration:
Mugatthaan amarndhu inidhu nokki agatthaanaam,
Inso linadhe aram.
current_meaning: A face that welcomes, a gaze that rests kindly on the other person, and sweet words that come up from inside rather than off the surface — that itself is virtue.
elementary_explanation: When someone talks to you while looking at their phone, even nice words feel cold. But when a person turns to you, smiles, actually looks at you, and means what they say — that feels completely different. This kural says that whole package isn't just being polite. It IS being good.
university_explanation: The couplet is structured as an ascending sequence of three organs of kindness: முகத்தான் (mugatthaan, by the face), நோக்கி (nokki, by the look), and அகத்தான் (agatthaan, from within). The claim in the final word is unusually strong — Valluvar does not say such conduct leads to அறம் (aram, virtue/dharma) or is a part of it, but that it is aram, full stop. Given that aram is the governing category of the entire first book of the Kural, encompassing householder duty, ascetic restraint and social justice, identifying it with a warm face and a heartfelt word is a striking democratisation of virtue: it makes the moral life available in every ordinary encounter, requiring neither wealth nor renunciation. The insistence that the word must arise அகத்தான் — from the interior — also forecloses the reading that this is mere etiquette.

tamil:
துன்புறூஉம் துவ்வாமை இல்லாகும் யார்மாட்டும்
இன்புறூஉம் இன்சொ லவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Thunburooum thuvvaamai illaagum yaarmaattum,
Inburooum inso lavarkku.
current_meaning: Those who speak words that gladden everyone they meet, without exception, will never be overtaken by the grinding poverty that brings misery.
elementary_explanation: Think of someone at school everybody likes because they're kind to everyone — not just their own friends. When that person needs help, ten people offer. Being warm to everybody builds up a kind of invisible savings account. This kural says people like that don't end up with nothing.
university_explanation: The key word is யார்மாட்டும் (yaarmaattum, 'toward anyone at all'), which universalises the obligation and rules out selective charm directed at the useful. துவ்வாமை (thuvvaamai) is a striking choice: it derives from துவ்வு (to eat/enjoy) and so denotes destitution specifically as the inability to consume or enjoy — want at the level of the body. Valluvar claims that the person who gives everyone the enjoyment (இன்புறூஉம், inburooum) of a kind word will not suffer the want of enjoyment. Commentators from Parimelazhagar onward have read this both prudentially (goodwill converts into material support) and karmically (the merit of universal kindness bears fruit). The verse also uses the elongated alapedai forms துன்புறூஉம் / இன்புறூஉம் to set the two states of misery and delight in exact metrical opposition.

tamil:
பணிவுடையன் இன்சொலன் ஆதல் ஒருவற்கு
அணியல்ல மற்றுப் பிற.
transliteration:
Panivudaiyan insolan aadhal oruvarku,
Aniyalla matrup pira.
current_meaning: To be humble and to speak kindly — that is a person's real ornament; nothing else deserves the name.
elementary_explanation: You can put on the nicest shoes and the coolest jacket and still have nobody want to sit with you. But if you're kind and you don't act like you're better than everyone, people want to be near you. This kural says humility and kind words are the jewellery that actually works.
university_explanation: அணி (ani) in Tamil poetic usage covers both physical ornament and rhetorical figure, so Valluvar's metaphor carries a faint irony: the true 'figure of speech' is not an embellishment of language but a quality of the speaker. The pairing of பணிவு (panivu, humility/bending) with இன்சொல் is deliberate — sweet speech without humility collapses into condescension, while humility without kind speech remains invisible. The closing அணியல்ல மற்றுப் பிற ('other things are not ornaments') is an absolute exclusion, and Tamil commentators note it as a rejection of the courtly display culture in which jewellery signified rank. The trope of speech-as-the-only-true-ornament is remarkably widespread: Bhartrihari's Sanskrit formulation is so close that some comparatists have argued for shared circulation of the image across the Deccan in the early centuries CE, though no dependency can be demonstrated.

tamil:
அல்லவை தேய அறம்பெருகும் நல்லவை
நாடி இனிய சொலின்.
transliteration:
Allavai theya arampperugum nallavai,
Naadi iniya solin.
current_meaning: If a person searches out what is genuinely good to say and then says it pleasantly, evil wears away and virtue grows.
elementary_explanation: It's like weeding a garden. Every time you plant something good — a kind, helpful word — there's a little less room for weeds. Do it often enough and the weeds shrink while the flowers spread. This kural says kind, useful words work on the world like that.
university_explanation: The verb நாடி (naadi, 'having sought out, investigated') is the hinge of the couplet and is easy to miss. Valluvar is not recommending spontaneous niceness but a deliberate search for what will actually benefit the hearer, delivered pleasantly. The two clauses form a causal pair with a striking agricultural logic: அல்லவை தேய ('evils wearing thin, eroding') and அறம் பெருகும் ('virtue swelling, increasing') — a single practice simultaneously depletes one and augments the other. This is one of the few places where Valluvar assigns speech a world-altering rather than merely personal effect, anticipating the argument of chapters 19 (on not slandering) and 20 (on avoiding useless words). The claim that gentle words can actually reduce the quantity of evil in the world finds its most dramatic mythic expression in Aeschylus and its clearest scriptural statement in Qur'an 41:34.

tamil:
நயன்ஈன்று நன்றி பயக்கும் பயன்ஈன்று
பண்பின் தலைப்பிரியாச் சொல்.
transliteration:
Nayan eendru nandri payakkum payan eendru,
Panbin thalaippiriyaach chol.
current_meaning: Words that give real benefit to the hearer and never step outside the bounds of good character bring the speaker both goodwill in this life and moral merit.
elementary_explanation: There's a difference between a friend who tells you what you want to hear and a friend who tells you something helpful, kindly. The second kind of talking does two jobs at once: it helps the other person, and it makes you a better person too. This kural is about that double win.
university_explanation: The couplet is built on a careful distinction between two returns: நயன் (nayan, goodwill, favour, social benefit accruing to the speaker) and நன்றி (nandri, here in its older sense of moral good or merit rather than gratitude). The condition for both is that the speech must be பண்பின் தலைப்பிரியா — literally 'not parting from the head of good character' — a striking idiom implying that speech remains tethered to the speaker's cultivated disposition rather than floating free as mere technique. This anticipates by some centuries the point Aristotle makes about ethos, that the most potent mode of persuasion is the character the speech itself displays. The doubled ஈன்று (eendru, 'having borne/given birth to') repeated in both lines gives the verse a generative, almost obstetric image: beneficial speech reproduces itself as both goodwill and merit.

tamil:
சிறுமையுள் நீங்கிய இன்சொல் மறுமையும்
இம்மையும் இன்பம் தரும்.
transliteration:
Sirumaiyul neengiya insol marumaiyum,
Immaiyum inbam tharum.
current_meaning: Kind words that carry no trace of meanness bring happiness both in this life and in the life to come.
elementary_explanation: Some people say something nice but slip a little insult inside it, like a stone hidden in a cake. This kural says the kind words that count are the ones with nothing mean tucked inside — and those are the ones that make you happy now and keep on paying you back later.
university_explanation: சிறுமை (sirumai) means smallness, and by extension pettiness, meanness or baseness; the phrase சிறுமையுள் நீங்கிய ('having departed from smallness') therefore screens out the backhanded compliment, the sweetly delivered slight, the kindness offered as a display of superiority. Valluvar then makes his only eschatological claim in the chapter, invoking the standard Tamil pairing இம்மை / மறுமை (immai / marumai, this birth and the next). The pairing is significant for the Kural's interpretive history: it has been read by Jain scholars as evidence of a rebirth framework, by Saiva commentators as reference to heaven, and by twentieth-century secular readers as a rhetorical intensifier meaning simply 'always'. The formula 'in this world and the next' is one of the most durable rhetorical structures in world ethics, recurring near-verbatim in the Dhammapada, the Gita and the Mishnah.

tamil:
இன்சொல் இனிதீன்றல் காண்பான் எவன்கொலோ
வன்சொல் வழங்கு வது.
transliteration:
Insol inidheendral kaanbaan evankolo,
Vansol vazhangu vadhu.
current_meaning: Someone who has seen for himself the pleasure kind words give — what on earth can he be thinking when he goes around dealing out harsh ones?
elementary_explanation: You already know how good it feels when someone is nice to you. So why would you ever be mean to someone else? You've already felt both sides. This kural is basically asking, with a raised eyebrow: what are you even doing?
university_explanation: This is the chapter's only rhetorical question, and Valluvar uses it for maximum force. எவன்கொலோ (evankolo) is an idiom of genuine puzzlement — 'whatever for?' — rather than condemnation, which makes the couplet feel less like a prohibition than an expression of bafflement. The argument's structure is a pure appeal to first-person evidence: the person addressed is a காண்பான், one who has himself seen and experienced the pleasure that kind words produce. Harsh speech is therefore presented not primarily as wicked but as irrational, a failure to reason from one's own experience to another's. This is precisely the logic of the Golden Rule in its negative form, and the verse's structure makes it the Kural's closest approach to that formula. The contrast pair இன்சொல் / வன்சொல் (sweet word / hard word) also sets up the culminating fruit-image of Kural 100.

tamil:
இனிய உளவாக இன்னாத கூறல்
கனிஇருப்பக் காய்கவர்ந் தற்று.
transliteration:
Iniya ulavaaga innaadha kooral,
Kani iruppak kaaikavarn dhatru.
current_meaning: To speak hurtful words when pleasant ones are right there for the taking is like grabbing at the unripe fruit while the ripe fruit hangs beside it.
elementary_explanation: Picture a tree with sweet ripe mangoes hanging low and hard green ones next to them. Nobody would reach past the sweet ones to bite a sour green one. But that's exactly what people do when they say something harsh when a kind thing would have worked just as well.
university_explanation: The chapter closes on its most famous image, and the comparison is chosen with care: கனி (kani, ripe fruit) and காய் (kaai, unripe fruit) come from the same tree at the same moment, so the choice costs nothing and requires no extra effort — which is exactly the point. உளவாக (ulavaaga, 'there being available') carries the weight: the pleasant words are already present and to hand. The verse thus completes the chapter's argument by removing the last excuse, since harsh speech can no longer be defended as necessary, cheaper, or more efficient. The kani/kaai contrast belongs to a wider Tamil poetic register of fruit imagery, and the comparative particle அற்று (atru, 'is like that') is the classical Tamil marker of simile. Strikingly, three other traditions independently reach for fruit or tree imagery at exactly this point — James on the fig and the vine, the Qur'an on the good and evil tree, Proverbs on apples of gold — suggesting how naturally the ethics of speech attracts the metaphor of cultivation.

tamil:
செய்யாமல் செய்த உதவிக்கு வையகமும்
வானகமும் ஆற்றல் அரிது.
transliteration:
Seyyaamal seydha udhavikku vaiyagamum
Vaanagamum aatral aridhu.
current_meaning: Help given to you when you had done nothing to earn it is so great that even the gift of earth and heaven together could hardly repay it.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a kid you barely know shares their lunch with you on a day you forgot yours, even though you never did anything for them. This kural says a kindness like that is so big that even if you gave them the whole world and the sky too, it still would not be enough to pay it back.
university_explanation: The chapter opens with its most extreme claim. Parimelazhagar reads செய்யாமல் செய்த உதவி as help rendered to someone who had done no prior service to the giver: a benefit that is not itself a repayment and therefore springs from pure goodwill. The predicate வையகமும் வானகமும் ஆற்றல் அரிது (earth and heaven can hardly equal it) deliberately places the debt beyond any possible exchange; if the terrestrial and celestial worlds together are inadequate, gratitude cannot be discharged by payment and must become a permanent disposition instead. This anticipates a problem that Aristotle (Nicomachean Ethics 8.14) and Seneca (De Beneficiis) would both recognise: a class of benefits, above all those from parents and gods, that no return can equal. Placing the chapter in the இல்லறவியல் (householder's section), immediately after Pleasant Speech, frames gratitude as a social virtue that sustains the web of reciprocity on which household and community life depend.

tamil:
காலத்தி னாற்செய்த நன்றி சிறிதெனினும்
ஞாலத்தின் மாணப் பெரிது.
transliteration:
Kaalaththinaal seydha nandri siridheninum
Gnaalaththin maanap peridhu.
current_meaning: A favour done at the moment of real need, however small in itself, is worth far more than the whole world.
elementary_explanation: If you are thirsty in the middle of a race and someone hands you one small cup of water, that cup feels more valuable than a whole shop full of drinks later. Help that comes right when you need it is the biggest kind of help, even if it is tiny.
university_explanation: The operative word is காலத்தினால், 'by reason of the time', that is, timeliness. Valluvar shifts the measure of a benefit from its quantity (சிறிதெனினும், 'though small') to its moment, and then inflates it past ஞாலம், the whole earth, with the intensifier மாண ('exceedingly'). Kurals 102 to 104 form a graded triad of hyperbolic comparisons (world, sea, palmyra palm), each isolating a different factor that magnifies a benefit: timing, disinterestedness, and the recipient's discernment. The underlying intuition is almost economic: the value of help peaks at the point of greatest need, which is why Solomon Pappaiah glosses the phrase as help given in our time of crisis. Aristotle records the same argument from the benefactor's side, noting that givers insist their help came 'in times of danger or similar need' (Nicomachean Ethics 8.13).

tamil:
பயன்தூக்கார் செய்த உதவி நயன்தூக்கின்
நன்மை கடலின் பெரிது.
transliteration:
Payandhookkaar seydha udhavi nayandhookkin
Nanmai kadalin peridhu.
current_meaning: When someone helps without calculating what they will get back, the goodness of that help, if you truly weigh it, is greater than the ocean.
elementary_explanation: Some people help you because they want something later, like a sticker trade. Others help just because they care. This kural says the second kind of help is bigger than the whole sea.
university_explanation: The couplet hinges on a pun on தூக்கு, 'to weigh': the benefactor is பயன்தூக்கார், one who does not weigh the return, while the recipient is invited to weigh (நயன்தூக்கின்) the help's goodness or love (நயன், from நயம்). Gratitude is thus framed as an act of moral appraisal that the giver refused to perform on his own behalf; the asymmetry is the point. Mu. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah gloss நயன் as the love (அன்பு) behind the act, so the 'sea' measures not the material help but the disinterested affection it expresses. This parallels the Bhagavad Gita's category of sattvic giving (17.20), made 'without expectation of return', and Aristotle's remark (Nicomachean Ethics 8.13) that it is noble to benefit another without a view to repayment even though most people prefer to receive. The kural quietly criticises transactional benevolence while insisting that recipients never take pure generosity lightly.

tamil:
தினைத்துணை நன்றி செயினும் பனைத்துணையாக்
கொள்வர் பயன்தெரி வார்.
transliteration:
Thinaiththunai nandri seyinum panaiththunaiyaak
Kolvar payantheri vaar.
current_meaning: Those who understand the value of kindness treat a favour as small as a millet seed as if it were as tall as a palm tree.
elementary_explanation: A millet seed is tiny, smaller than a grain of rice. A palm tree is huge. A grateful person takes even a tiny kindness, like someone lending a pencil, and treats it like something huge.
university_explanation: தினை (foxtail millet, among the smallest grains in the Tamil diet) and பனை (the palmyra, the tallest and most useful tree of the Tamil landscape) form one of the Kural's most memorable scale contrasts; the same pair recurs in Kural 433, where those who fear disgrace treat a fault the size of millet as if it were the size of a palm. The subject பயன்தெரிவார், 'those who discern the fruit or benefit', makes gratitude a cognitive virtue: the grateful person perceives consequences that the literal size of the gift conceals. Kalaignar's gloss exploits the palmyra's many uses (fruit, leaf, timber, sap) to suggest that a small help ramifies into manifold benefit. The same inversion of scale appears in the Gospel's widow's mite, in the Talmud's 'good guest' of Berakhot 58a, and in Seneca's argument that a benefit lies in the intention rather than in the object given.

tamil:
உதவி வரைத்தன்று உதவி உதவி
செயப்பட்டார் சால்பின் வரைத்து.
transliteration:
Udhavi varaiththandru udhavi udhavi
Seyappattaar saalbin varaiththu.
current_meaning: The worth of a favour is not set by the favour itself; it is set by the character of the person who received it.
elementary_explanation: If a friend gives you a small gift, how much you give back is not just about the size of their gift. It is about what kind of person you are. A really good-hearted person gives back even more than they got.
university_explanation: Built on a fourfold repetition of உதவி (help), the couplet admits two readings. Parimelazhagar, followed by Mu. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah, takes the first உதவி as the return-favour: requital is not bounded by the size of the original help but by the சால்பு (nobility, fullness of character) of the one who was helped, so a noble recipient repays abundantly. Kalaignar reads it evaluatively: the value of a help is assessed according to the recipient's worth. Both readings converge on the claim that gratitude measures the recipient rather than balancing a ledger, linking this chapter to the later chapter on சான்றாண்மை (perfect character). Aristotle frames the same dispute, whether to measure a service by its utility to the receiver or by the benevolence of the giver (Nicomachean Ethics 8.13), and Cicero, citing Hesiod, urges us to imitate fertile fields that return more than they receive (De Officiis 1.48).

tamil:
மறவற்க மாசற்றார் கேண்மை துறவற்க
துன்பத்துள் துப்பாயார் நட்பு.
transliteration:
Maravarka maasatraar kenmai thuravarka
Thunbaththul thuppaayaar natpu.
current_meaning: Never forget the friendship of people who are pure-hearted, and never abandon the friendship of those who stood by you as your strength in hard times.
elementary_explanation: Some friends are simply good people, so don't forget them. And some friends helped you when you were sad or in trouble, so never walk away from them, even after things get better for you.
university_explanation: The couplet is built as two parallel prohibitions, மறவற்க ('do not forget') and துறவற்க ('do not forsake'), each governing a class of relationship: the கேண்மை (bond) of the மாசற்றார் (the stainless) and the நட்பு (friendship) of those who became துப்பு (strength, support) in துன்பம் (distress). Commentators take the first half to concern those free of fault in knowledge and conduct and the second those who helped in adversity; the chapter thereby widens gratitude from discrete favours to durable relationships. The verb துறத்தல், the same root used for renunciation, suggests that abandoning a former helper is a kind of moral apostasy.
