The theme anticipates the Kural's later friendship chapters (79-83), where adversity is repeatedly named as the true test of a friend.

tamil:
எழுமை எழுபிறப்பும் உள்ளுவர் தங்கண்
விழுமந் துடைத்தவர் நட்பு.
transliteration:
Ezhumai ezhupirappum ulluvar thangan
Vizhuman thudaiththavar natpu.
current_meaning: The good remember, through all their seven births, the friendship of those who wiped away their sorrow.
elementary_explanation: If someone wiped away your tears when you were really hurting, you should remember them for a very, very long time. The kural says: for seven whole lifetimes!
university_explanation: விழுமம் denotes grave affliction, and துடைத்தல், 'to wipe away', evokes the wiping of tears, an image that G. U. Pope's verse translation foregrounds. எழுமை எழுபிறப்பும் is variously parsed: traditional commentary reads it within the South Asian doctrine of rebirth as 'through sevenfold births', while modern commentators such as Kalaignar treat it as hyperbole meaning 'without any limit of time'. Either way, the couplet turns gratitude from a transaction into a form of memory (உள்ளுவர், 'they will keep in mind') whose duration exceeds a single life. The motif of long-lived or even inherited gratitude, such as David's kindness to Jonathan's son, Rama's avowed debt to Hanuman, and the Buddha's thought of the five companions after his awakening, shows how widely traditions have treated rescuers as creditors whose claim outlives the moment of rescue.

tamil:
நன்றி மறப்பது நன்றன்று நன்றல்லது
அன்றே மறப்பது நன்று.
transliteration:
Nandri marappadhu nandrandru nandralladhu
Andre marappadhu nandru.
current_meaning: It is not good to forget a kindness done to you; but it is good to forget a wrong done to you on the very same day.
elementary_explanation: Keep the good things people do for you in your memory box forever. But if someone is mean to you, try to let it go before you go to bed that night.
university_explanation: The couplet is a celebrated piece of Valluvar's wordplay, circling the root நன்று (good) through நன்றி (a benefit), நன்றன்று (not good) and நன்றல்லது (what is not good, i.e. an injury), and pivoting on அன்றே, 'that very day'. It proposes an asymmetric economy of memory: benefits are to be retained indefinitely, injuries released at once. Ethically, this protects gratitude from being eroded by later grievances, a theme the next couplet (109) develops; psychologically, it anticipates modern research that treats gratitude and forgiveness as complementary dispositions. The instruction to let go of a wrong 'that very day' closely parallels Ephesians 4:26 ('let not the sun go down upon your wrath'), while the Psalmist's 'forget not all his benefits' supplies the other half of the Kural's pairing.

tamil:
கொன்றன்ன இன்னா செயினும் அவர்செய்த
ஒன்றுநன்று உள்ளக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Kondranna innaa seyinum avarseydha
Ondrunandru ullak kedum.
current_meaning: Even if someone who once helped you later hurts you as badly as if they had killed you, that hurt fades the moment you remember the one good thing they did.
elementary_explanation: Suppose a friend who once caught you when you were falling later does something that really hurts you. If you remember the time they caught you, the hurt shrinks. One good memory can melt a big hurt.
university_explanation: கொன்றன்ன இன்னா, 'an injury like killing', is the strongest possible provocation, and the verb கெடும் ('will perish') leaves its subject implicit: commentators take it to be the injury, or the pain and resentment it causes, that is destroyed merely by recalling (உள்ள) one (ஒன்று) earlier good (நன்று). The kural thus makes gratitude an active remedy rather than merely a debt: memory of a past benefit is prescribed as the means of dissolving present grievance. Valmiki's portrait of Rama in Ayodhya Kanda 2.1.11, gladdened by a single good deed and forgetting a hundred wrongs, is close enough to suggest a shared South Asian ethical ideal. A concrete legal-historical parallel is the Prophet Muhammad's pardon of Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a, whose betrayal was weighed against his earlier service at Badr.

tamil:
எந்நன்றி கொன்றார்க்கும் உய்வுண்டாம் உய்வில்லை
செய்ந்நன்றி கொன்ற மகற்கு.
transliteration:
Ennandri kondraarkkum uyvundaam uyvillai
Seynnandri kondra magarku.
current_meaning: Those who have destroyed any other virtue may still find a way to be saved, but there is no salvation for the one who destroys gratitude for a kindness done to him.
elementary_explanation: People can make lots of mistakes and still fix them. But this kural says the one thing that is almost impossible to fix is being ungrateful to someone who helped you, so that is the one mistake you should never make.
university_explanation: The chapter closes with its severest verdict. Mu. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah, following the traditional commentary, read the first நன்றி as அறம் in general ('whoever has killed any virtue'), against which செய்ந்நன்றி கொன்ற மகன், the man who has 'killed' a benefit by forgetting it or returning harm for it, stands uniquely without உய்வு (escape, deliverance). The idea has deep roots in Tamil and Sanskrit tradition: the Sangam anthology Puranānūru (poem 34) is commonly cited alongside this kural for declaring that there is no escape for those who destroy a benefit, and Valmiki's Kishkindha Kanda (4.34.12) says atonement is ordained for cow-slayers, drinkers, thieves and vow-breakers but not for the kṛtaghna, the ingrate. Outside South Asia, Cicero held that no duty is more imperative than proving one's gratitude (De Officiis 1.47), and Hume chose ingratitude as the most horrid and unnatural of crimes (Treatise 3.1.1). This agreement suggests that ingratitude was treated not as one vice among many but as the destruction of the reciprocity on which moral community rests.

tamil:
தகுதி எனவொன்று நன்றே பகுதியால்
பாற்பட்டு ஒழுகப் பெறின்.
transliteration:
Thakudhi enavondru nandre pakudhiyaal
Paarpattu ozhukap perin.
current_meaning: The virtue called “fitness” — impartiality — is truly good when a person acts rightly and fairly toward every group of people alike, whether enemies, strangers or friends.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a referee who calls the game the same way whether the player is his best friend, a stranger, or someone he doesn’t like. That fairness to everyone is what this kural calls a truly good quality.
university_explanation: The chapter opens by naming impartiality with the word தகுதி (thakudhi, “fitness, propriety, worthiness”), implying that fairness is not one virtue among many but the very measure of whether a person is fit to be trusted. The key phrase பகுதியால் பாற்பட்டு (“keeping to what is due in each division”) was read by the medieval commentator Parimelazhagar, and after him by modern commentators such as Solomon Pappaiah and Karunanidhi, as the threefold division of people into enemies, strangers (neutrals) and friends; the test of justice is that the same standard applies across all three. Placing this chapter in the Illaraviyal (the householder’s section) signals that Valluvar sees impartiality as an everyday domestic and civic duty, not only a king’s or judge’s duty (royal justice is treated separately in chapter 55, செங்கோன்மை). The idea parallels the classical definition of justice as rendering to each their due, and Aristotle’s observation that justice, unlike the other virtues, is directed essentially toward others.

tamil:
செப்பம் உடையவன் ஆக்கஞ் சிதைவின்றி
எச்சத்திற் கேமாப்பு உடைத்து.
transliteration:
Seppam udaiyavan aakkanj sidhaivindri
Echchaththirku emaappu udaiththu.
current_meaning: The prosperity of an upright, impartial person does not crumble away; it lasts and becomes a secure support even for their descendants.
elementary_explanation: Think of a house built on strong, straight foundations. It doesn’t fall down; the grandchildren can still live in it. Wealth earned fairly is like that house, and it keeps protecting the family.
university_explanation: செப்பம் (seppam, “straightness, rectitude”) is used here as a synonym for naduvu nilaimai, and the couplet makes a claim about consequences: the ஆக்கம் (aakkam, “increase, prosperity”) of the just person is சிதைவின்றி (“without disintegration”) and furnishes ஏமாப்பு (emaappu, “security, protection”) to the எச்சம் (echcham, “what remains after one”), which the commentators read as descendants or posterity. The point is intergenerational: unjust gain may be large but brittle, while justly earned wealth is durable. The idea that righteousness is an inheritance for children’s children is widespread, found in Proverbs, the Psalms, the Qur’anic story of the orphans’ buried treasure, and Hesiod’s claim that the truthful man’s “generation” prospers. The word echcham reappears in Kural 114, where its meaning (offspring or legacy) becomes a matter of commentarial debate.

tamil:
நன்றே தரினும் நடுவிகந்தாம் ஆக்கத்தை
அன்றே யொழிய விடல்.
transliteration:
Nandre tharinum naduvikandhaam aakkaththai
Andre yozhiya vidal.
current_meaning: Even if it seems to bring only good, any gain that comes from abandoning fairness should be let go that very day.
elementary_explanation: Suppose you find out you won a prize only because the judge was your uncle and cheated for you. Even though the prize is nice, the right thing is to give it back right away.
university_explanation: The couplet anticipates the objection that injustice might sometimes pay: நன்றே தரினும் (“even if it yields only good”). Valluvar’s answer is categorical. Gain acquired by நடு இகந்து (“transgressing the middle/the just mean”) must be relinquished அன்றே (“that very day”), with no waiting to see whether it turns out well. The emphasis on immediacy suggests a psychological insight: ill-gotten advantage becomes harder to renounce the longer one holds it. The ethic parallels Socrates’ insistence in the Apology that wealth pursued at the cost of the soul is shameful, the Qur’anic ban on consuming others’ property unjustly, and Hesiod’s warning that seized wealth stays only “for a little time.” Philosophically it is a deontological stance: the injustice of the means cannot be redeemed by the goodness of the outcome.

tamil:
தக்கார் தகவிலர் என்பது அவரவர்
எச்சத்தாற் காணப்ப படும்.
transliteration:
Thakkaar thakavilar enbadhu avaravar
Echchaththaar kaanappa padum.
current_meaning: Whether a person was just or unjust is revealed by what they leave behind: the good name or ill fame (or, in the older reading, the children) that outlives them.
elementary_explanation: You can tell what kind of gardener someone was by what is still growing in the garden after they leave. People are like that too: what remains after them shows whether they were fair.
university_explanation: The couplet turns on எச்சம் (echcham, “that which remains”). Parimelazhagar reads it as offspring: the worth of the just is visible in good descendants, a reading reflected in G. U. Pope’s translation (“By each one’s offspring shall the truth be clear”). Mu. Varadarasanar and Karunanidhi instead read it as the reputation, praise or blame, that remains after death, while Solomon Pappaiah combines wealth, fame and the conduct of one’s children. Either way the claim is that a verdict on a life’s justice can only be given in retrospect, from its durable effects. This echoes Solon’s advice to Croesus (in Herodotus) to call no one happy until their end is seen, Jesus’ “by their fruits ye shall know them,” and the hadith that a righteous child is among the deeds that continue after death. Note on the text: all three consulted editions (thirukkural.net, ytamizh.com, Project Madurai) print காணப்ப படும்; many printed editions give காணப் படும். The meaning is unaffected.

tamil:
கேடும் பெருக்கமும் இல்லல்ல நெஞ்சத்துக்
கோடாமை சான்றோர்க் கணி.
transliteration:
Kedum perukkamum illalla nenjaththuk
Kodaamai saandrork kani.
current_meaning: Loss and gain are bound to come in every life; the ornament of the truly noble is a heart that does not bend away from fairness in either.
elementary_explanation: Some days you win, some days you lose; that happens to everyone. A good person plays fair on both kinds of days, and that fairness is their best jewel.
university_explanation: The first line states a plain fact: கேடும் பெருக்கமும் இல்லல்ல (“ruin and increase are not things that do not exist”), that is, they are inevitable. Parimelazhagar attributes them to past deeds (ūḻ), which is reflected in Pope’s “not mere accident” and Solomon Pappaiah’s “already ordained.” Given that fortune is outside our control, the only thing that distinguishes the சான்றோர் (saandror, “the accomplished/noble”) is நெஞ்சத்துக் கோடாமை, “not bending in the heart.” The verb கோடு (“to bend, to be crooked”) is the key image of the chapter and returns in Kurals 118 and 119. The ethic is close to Stoic doctrine, which separates externals from the governing faculty, and to the Gita’s samatva (evenness in gain and loss). The refrain கோடாமை சான்றோர்க்கு அணி is repeated word for word in Kural 118.

tamil:
கெடுவல்யான் என்பது அறிகதன் நெஞ்சம்
நடுவொரீஇ அல்ல செயின்.
transliteration:
Keduval yaan enbadhu arika than nenjam
Naduvoreei alla seyin.
current_meaning: If a person’s heart leaves fairness and turns to wrongdoing, let them recognize it as a sure sign: “I am heading for ruin.”
elementary_explanation: When a car starts drifting out of its lane, a warning beeps. This kural says that when your heart starts wanting to be unfair, that is your warning beep: trouble is coming if you don’t steer back.
university_explanation: The couplet is written as an internal monologue: கெடுவல் யான் (“I shall perish”) is what one should say to oneself the moment the heart நடு ஒரீஇ (“having abandoned the middle”) turns toward அல்ல (“what is not [right]”). Commentators differ on emphasis. Varadarasanar and Karunanidhi stress the intention itself as the omen (“if the heart even thinks of it”), while Pope renders it “let man impending ruin’s sign discern.” Either way, injustice is presented as self-destructive, not merely harmful to others. This matches the Manusmriti’s maxim that violated justice destroys the violator, the Qur’anic warning to David that following desire in judgment leads astray, and Plato’s argument that injustice is a disease of the soul.

tamil:
கெடுவாக வையாது உலகம் நடுவாக
நன்றிக்கண் தங்கியான் தாழ்வு.
transliteration:
Keduvaaga vaiyaadhu ulagam naduvaaga
Nandrikkan thangiyaan thaazhvu.
current_meaning: When a person who stays fair and holds to what is right becomes poor, the world does not regard that as a downfall.
elementary_explanation: If a shopkeeper loses money because she refused to cheat anyone, people don’t think of her as a failure. They respect her even more.
university_explanation: Kural 117 answers an objection that Kural 112 might invite: what if the just person does not prosper? Valluvar grants that the one who நடுவாக நன்றிக்கண் தங்கியான் (“abides in goodness, keeping to the middle”) may suffer தாழ்வு (“lowness, decline, poverty”), but insists the உலகம் will not regard it as கேடு (“ruin”). Here “the world” means the wise or discerning, as Pope (“wise man’s sight”) and Pappaiah (“the great”) make explicit. Social esteem is separated from material fortune: honour tracks justice, not wealth. The theme recurs across traditions: Proverbs’ “better is the poor that walketh in his uprightness,” the Beatitude for those persecuted for righteousness, Socrates’ poverty for the sake of his mission, and the Hindu legend of Harishchandra, who lost everything rather than break his word.

tamil:
சமன்செய்து சீர்தூக்குங் கோல்போல் அமைந்தொருபால்
கோடாமை சான்றோர்க் கணி.
transliteration:
Saman seydhu seerthookkung kolpol amaindhorupaal
Kodaamai saandrork kani.
current_meaning: Like a balance-beam that first sets itself level and then weighs things exactly, the noble person stays steady and does not lean to either side; this is their true ornament.
elementary_explanation: A good weighing scale sits perfectly flat before you put anything on it, then shows the true weight, no matter whose apples they are. A fair person is like that scale: steady and not tipping toward anyone.
university_explanation: This is the chapter’s central image. The துலாக்கோல் (tulaakkol, balance-beam) first சமன்செய்து (“makes itself even”), then சீர்தூக்கும் (“weighs rightly”), and does not ஒருபால் கோடாமை (“incline to one side”). Varadarasanar and Pappaiah stress the two-stage sequence: the judge must first be internally level, free of prior bias, and only then evaluate. That is a sharp account of impartiality as a disposition as well as a procedure. The scale is a near-universal emblem of justice: Zeus’s golden scales in Homer, the Qur’anic mīzān, the “just balances” of Leviticus, and the Dhammapada’s sage who weighs good and evil “as if holding a balance-scale.” Aristotle’s description of the judge as “animate justice” and “intermediate” states the same idea philosophically. The second line repeats the refrain of Kural 115, linking inner steadiness under fortune to outer impartiality in judgment.

tamil:
சொற்கோட்டம் இல்லது செப்பம் ஒருதலையா
உட்கோட்டம் இன்மை பெறின்.
transliteration:
Sorkottam illadhu seppam orudhalaiyaa
Utkottam inmai perin.
current_meaning: Speech free of crookedness counts as true fairness only when the heart itself is firmly free of any crookedness or bias.
elementary_explanation: A shiny apple can still be rotten inside. Saying fair-sounding words isn’t enough; your heart has to be fair on the inside too, and then your words will be truly straight.
university_explanation: The couplet pairs சொற்கோட்டம் (“crookedness of word”) with உட்கோட்டம் (“inner crookedness”) and makes the first depend on the second: straight speech is செப்பம் (rectitude) only if one ஒருதலையா (“definitely, without fail”) has an unbent inner state. The target is the sophisticated partiality of someone who says the right things while privately favouring one side. That concern fits a chapter aimed at those who arbitrate, give testimony or advise. Commentators read it both ways. Varadarasanar treats inner straightness as the condition, while Pappaiah and Karunanidhi treat straight speech as its natural result. The same principle, that honest speech flows from an honest heart, appears in Jesus’ “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh,” Achilles’ contempt for the man “who says one thing while he hides another in his heart,” and Plato’s distinction between the lie in words and the “true lie” in the soul.

tamil:
வாணிகம் செய்வார்க்கு வாணிகம் பேணிப்
பிறவும் தமபோல் செயின்.
transliteration:
Vaanigam seyvaarkku vaanigam penip
Piravum thamapol seyin.
current_meaning: For those who trade, the true way of trade is to guard and deal with other people’s goods and interests as carefully as their own.
elementary_explanation: A good shopkeeper weighs your rice as carefully as if it were for her own family, and charges you the same fair price she’d want to pay herself. That’s what honest business means.
university_explanation: The chapter closes by applying impartiality to commerce, the everyday setting where people most often weigh and measure for one another. பிறவும் தமபோல் (“others’ [goods] as their own”) is the principle: the merchant must take no more and give no less than they would accept if the roles were reversed. Parimelazhagar notes the scale imagery carried over from Kural 118, since trade literally involves weighing. The doubled வாணிகம் (“trade … trade”) is emphatic: only this is real trade, and anything else is disguised theft. Parallels include the Qur’anic curse on those who give short measure, the Talmudic tradition that the first question at the heavenly judgment is “Did you conduct business faithfully?”, Hesiod’s counsel to give fair measure “or better,” and Kant’s honest shopkeeper who charges a child the same as anyone else. Kant adds that honesty practised only because it pays is not yet fully moral, which fits the Kural’s demand for inner straightness in Kural 119.

tamil:
அடக்கம் அமரருள் உய்க்கும் அடங்காமை
ஆரிருள் உய்த்து விடும்.
transliteration:
Adakkam amararul uykkum adangaamai
Aarirul uyththu vidum.
current_meaning: Self-restraint raises a person into the company of the gods; the lack of it drives him into a darkness so thick there is no escaping it.
elementary_explanation: Picture two staircases. One climbs up to a bright room full of wise, kind people; the other goes down into a dark basement with no lights. Every time you hold yourself back from doing something wrong, you climb one step up. Every time you just do whatever you feel like, you slip one step down.
university_explanation: Valluvar opens the chapter by setting the stakes in the starkest possible terms: amarar (the immortals, the devas) versus aar-irul (a darkness that is ‘hard to bear’ or ‘dense’), which the medieval commentator Parimelazhagar glosses as a particular hell. Parimelazhagar defines adakkam as the condition in which body, speech and mind (mey, mozhi, manam) do not stray into wrong paths, and explains that the chapter follows ‘Impartiality’ because one who sees his own faults as clearly as others’ will naturally restrain himself. Modern commentators such as Karunanidhi read the couplet in this-worldly terms — restraint earns undying renown, indiscipline darkens life itself — showing how the couplet supports both a religious and a secular reading. Its two-path structure, one road upward and one downward, is among the most widespread forms in world ethical literature, from the Dhammapada’s ‘path to the Deathless’ to Paul’s sowing to the flesh or the Spirit.

tamil:
காக்க பொருளா அடக்கத்தை ஆக்கம்
அதனினூஉங் கில்லை உயிர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Kaakka porulaa adakkaththai aakkam
Adhaninoovung killai uyirkku.
current_meaning: Guard self-restraint as you would guard a treasure, for no living being has any greater source of good than this.
elementary_explanation: People lock their money in a safe so nobody can take it. This kural says self-control is worth even more than money, so you should protect it just as carefully. You can lose toys or money, but if you hold on to your self-control, it keeps you good.
university_explanation: The key word is porulaa, ‘as wealth’ or ‘as a thing of real value’; Parimelazhagar glosses it as uruthip porul, an ultimate or assured good. The couplet turns ordinary economics upside down: restraint is not a sacrifice that costs us something but an asset (aakkam, ‘growth, prosperity’) that must be actively guarded (kaakka). That implies it can be lost or stolen, presumably by the passions. Parimelazhagar notes that uyir (‘living being’) here means human life in particular, since only humans can understand restraint and benefit from it. The idea that inner self-command is the truest possession has close relatives in the Stoic distinction between what is ‘up to us’ and what is not, and in the Mishnah’s redefinition of the mighty and the rich.

tamil:
செறிவறிந்து சீர்மை பயக்கும் அறிவறிந்து
ஆற்றின் அடங்கப் பெறின்.
transliteration:
Serivarindhu seermai payakkum arivarindhu
Aatrin adangap perin.
current_meaning: If a person understands that restraint is itself wisdom and lives restrained in the right way, that restraint will be recognized by the good and will bring him distinction.
elementary_explanation: Think of a kid who quietly does the right thing in class without showing off. At first nobody seems to notice, but the teacher does, and soon everyone respects that kid. Quiet goodness gets noticed in the end.
university_explanation: The couplet turns on two uses of arindhu (‘having known’). In arivarindhu, the person first understands what true knowledge is; Parimelazhagar reads this as grasping that restraint itself is our wisdom. In serivarindhu, that restraint comes to be known and recognized, by the wise, in Parimelazhagar’s reading. The result is seermai, excellence or eminence. The qualifier aatrin (‘in the proper way’) rules out showy or grudging restraint. Manakkudavar adds a sensory reading: one must know the five sense-objects (taste, sight, touch, sound, smell) and restrain the five organs that seek them. Joining knowledge to restraint echoes the Delphic ‘Know thyself,’ which Greek thought tied to sophrosyne, and Aristotle’s view that the temperate person desires ‘as reason directs.’

tamil:
நிலையின் திரியாது அடங்கியான் தோற்றம்
மலையினும் மாணப் பெரிது.
transliteration:
Nilaiyin thiriyaadhu adangiyaan thotram
Malaiyinum maanap peridhu.
current_meaning: The stature of one who stays restrained, never swerving from his proper path in life, towers even higher than a mountain.
elementary_explanation: A mountain stays put no matter how hard the wind blows. A person who stays calm and humble and keeps doing the right thing, without bragging, looks even ‘taller’ to others than a mountain.
university_explanation: Parimelazhagar reads nilai (‘station’) as the householder’s way of life, which fits the couplet’s place in the Illaraviyal (the section on domestic virtue). He takes ‘restraint without swerving’ to mean self-governance while still legitimately using the senses: disciplined participation in ordinary life, not ascetic withdrawal. Manakkudavar instead glosses nilai as one’s varnashrama duty. Thotram, ‘appearance’ or ‘stature,’ is read by Solomon Pappaiah as the impression such a person leaves in others’ minds, and the paradox is deliberate: the one who lowers himself appears the loftiest. The mountain works as an image of both height and immovability, which invites comparison with the Stoic promontory and the Buddhist unshaken rock.

tamil:
எல்லார்க்கும் நன்றாம் பணிதல் அவருள்ளும்
செல்வர்க்கே செல்வம் தகைத்து.
transliteration:
Ellaarkkum nandraam panidhal avarullum
Selvarkke selvam thakaiththu.
current_meaning: Humility is good for everyone, but in the wealthy it shines as a second kind of wealth.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a kid with the coolest new bike who still lets others ride it and never brags. Everyone likes that kid even more. Being humble when you have a lot is like having a bonus treasure on top of everything else.
university_explanation: Panidhal (‘bowing, humility’) makes explicit the social side of adakkam. Parimelazhagar explains why the rich are singled out: learning and noble birth already tend to restrain a person, so humility in the learned or well-born does not stand out, but wealth naturally breeds pride (perumitham). Humility in the rich is therefore especially striking, a ‘wealth added to wealth’ (selvam thakaiththu). He also points out that couplets 121–125 treat restraint in general, while 126 turns to bodily restraint, 127–129 to restraint of speech, and 130 to restraint of mind. The couplet reflects a view found in many traditions that prosperity, more than hardship, is the real test of character.

tamil:
ஒருமையுள் ஆமைபோல் ஐந்தடக்கல் ஆற்றின்
எழுமையும் ஏமாப் புடைத்து.
transliteration:
Orumaiyul aamaipol aindhadakkal aatrin
Ezhumaiyum emaap pudaiththu.
current_meaning: If, in this one life, a person can draw in his five senses the way a tortoise draws in its limbs, that power will guard him through seven births.
elementary_explanation: A turtle pulls its head and four legs into its shell when danger comes. We have five senses: eyes, ears, nose, tongue and skin. If we can ‘pull them in’ when they want something harmful, we are protected just like the turtle in its shell.
university_explanation: The tortoise image (aamai) also appears in Bhagavad Gita 2.58 and in the Pali Kumma Sutta, which points to a shared South Asian stock of contemplative imagery rather than direct borrowing. Parimelazhagar explains the simile exactly: the tortoise withdraws its five members (four legs and head) so that harm cannot get in, and a person should restrain the five senses so that sin cannot get in. He classes this couplet as teaching bodily restraint (meyyadakkam). The contrast of orumai (‘one birth’) and ezhumai (‘seven births’) draws on karma doctrine: effort in one life gives a safeguard (emaappu, ‘protection, fortress’) across many lives, though Karunanidhi secularizes it as ‘for all time.’ The tortoise does not destroy its limbs; it withdraws and extends them at will, so the ideal is mastery of the senses, not mutilation of them.

tamil:
யாகாவா ராயினும் நாகாக்க காவாக்கால்
சோகாப்பர் சொல்லிழுக்குப் பட்டு.
transliteration:
Yaakaavaa raayinum naakaakka kaavaakkaal
Sokaappar sollizhukkup pattu.
current_meaning: Whatever else you fail to guard, guard your tongue; those who don’t will come to grief, caught in the faults of their own words.
elementary_explanation: If you can only remember one rule, remember this: watch what you say. A friend who blurts out a secret or says something mean in anger can lose friends in a second. Even if you mess up other things, keeping your words kind protects you.
university_explanation: The couplet performs its own lesson in sound: the syllable kaa (‘guard’) recurs in yaa-kaavaar, naa-kaakka, kaavaak-kaal and so-kaappar, which makes the verse itself an exercise in controlled, measured speech. Parimelazhagar treats sokaappar (‘they will grieve’) as a single verb, like allaappar, and reads yaa (‘whatever’) as meaning ‘all things without exception.’ This couplet opens the three-verse unit on restraint of speech (mozhi adakkam, 127–129). Its claim that the tongue ranks above every other thing needing guard is a striking priority that other traditions also make: the Hadith pairs the tongue with chastity as the key to Paradise, and the Epistle of James calls the untamed tongue a fire.

tamil:
ஒன்றானுந் தீச்சொல் பொருட்பயன் உண்டாயின்
நன்றாகா தாகி விடும்.
transliteration:
Ondraanum theechchol porutpayan undaayin
Nandraakaa thaaki vidum.
current_meaning: If even a single harmful word causes harm through what it means, all the good a person has done turns to no good.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a big glass of milk with just one drop of poison in it. You can’t drink any of it now. In the same way, one really mean word can spoil lots of kind things you have said and done.
university_explanation: Parimelazhagar identifies ‘evil words’ (theechchol) as falsehood, slander (kuralai) and harsh speech, and reads the couplet to mean that if even one harm reaches another person through such words, the good earned by all one’s other virtues is turned to evil. Manakkudavar offers a subtler alternative: even a single word that sounds sweet but carries a harmful meaning (porutpayan) makes the speech bad. Karunanidhi’s image of a drop of poison in a pot of milk captures the moral asymmetry: harm is not simply offset by good but contaminates it. That puts the Kural at odds with purely additive ‘merit ledgers’ and aligns it with Ecclesiastes’ dead flies in the perfumer’s ointment.

tamil:
தீயினாற் சுட்டபுண் உள்ளாறும் ஆறாதே
நாவினாற் சுட்ட வடு.
transliteration:
Theeyinaar suttapun ullaarum aaraadhe
Naavinaar sutta vadu.
current_meaning: A wound burned by fire heals within, but the scar burned by the tongue never heals.
elementary_explanation: If you touch a hot stove, it hurts a lot, but in a week or two it heals. If someone says something really hurtful to you, you might remember it for years. Words can burn deeper than fire.
university_explanation: Parimelazhagar notes Valluvar’s careful word choice: the fire-burn is called pun (a wound, which heals), while the tongue-burn is called vadu (a scar, which stays). He classifies the couplet as vetrumai alankaram, a figure of contrast: fire and harsh words share the act of burning, but because harsh words never heal they are shown to be worse than fire. The phrase ul aarum (‘heals within’) concedes that a fire-burn may leave an outward mark while the inner hurt fades; with verbal wounds the reverse holds. This is among the most widely quoted of all kurals, and its near-twin in the Mahabharata’s counsel of Vidura shows how old and widespread the insight is. Modern research on the lasting psychological effects of verbal abuse gives it contemporary resonance.

tamil:
கதங்காத்துக் கற்றடங்கல் ஆற்றுவான் செவ்வி
அறம்பார்க்கும் ஆற்றின் நுழைந்து.
transliteration:
Kadhangaaththuk katradangal aatruvaan sevvi
Arampaarkkum aatrin nuzhaindhu.
current_meaning: Virtue itself enters the path of one who guards against anger, gains learning and is able to stay restrained, and waits there for the right moment to meet him.
elementary_explanation: Usually we have to go looking for good things. But if you learn a lot, stay calm when you’re angry, and stay humble, goodness comes looking for you, like a friend waiting at your door.
university_explanation: The closing couplet personifies Aram (Virtue; Parimelazhagar calls it ‘the deity of Dharma’) as a suitor who enters a person’s path and waits for his sevvi, the opportune moment when his mind, speech and face are gracious enough to be approached. This reverses the usual quest: instead of the seeker pursuing virtue, virtue pursues the restrained person. The condition has three parts: katham kaaththu (guarding against anger), katru (having learned) and adangal aatruvaan (being capable of restraint). Manakkudavar adds that the learned must also restrain the pride their learning can breed. Parimelazhagar classes this couplet as restraint of mind (manavadakkam), which completes the body–speech–mind triad around which the chapter’s second half is built. The pairing of anger control with learning parallels the Talmudic teaching that anger drives wisdom out of the sage.

tamil:
ஒழுக்கம் விழுப்பந் தரலான் ஒழுக்கம்
உயிரினும் ஓம்பப் படும்.
transliteration:
Ozhukkam vizhuppam tharalaan ozhukkam
Uyirinum oampap padum.
current_meaning: Because right conduct is what raises a person to true excellence, it must be guarded even more carefully than life itself.
elementary_explanation: Think of your good behavior as the most precious treasure you own, even more precious than your own body. It is what makes people trust and respect you, so you protect it more than anything else.
university_explanation: The chapter opens with a deliberately extreme ranking: ozhukkam (conduct, from ozhuku, ‘to proceed along a course’) is to be guarded (ompa) above uyir, life itself. The reason clause, vizhuppam tharalaan (‘because it confers eminence’), grounds the claim in what conduct produces rather than in divine command; bare life, as Pope's rendering notes, is something ‘all men share’, while conduct is what distinguishes. The word ozhukkam frames the first line at both ends, so the verse itself performs the act of guarding. Parimelazhagar reads ozhukkam as the conduct proper to one's station, whereas modern commentators (Varadarasanar, Karunanidhi) make it universal. The idea that some values outrank survival recurs widely, from Socrates' refusal to weigh life against right action to the rabbinic rule that certain sins must be refused even on pain of death.

tamil:
பரிந்தோம்பிக் காக்க ஒழுக்கம் தெரிந்தோம்பித்
தேரினும் அஃதே துணை.
transliteration:
Parindhoambik kaakka ozhukkam therindhoambith
Therinum aqdhe thunai.
current_meaning: Guard your conduct with care, even when it costs you effort. Weigh every other option, and you will find that conduct alone is the companion that truly stays with you.
elementary_explanation: Imagine testing every toy, game and friend to find the one that will stay with you forever. Valluvar says that after checking everything, the one thing that never leaves you is being good, so take good care of it.
university_explanation: Two phrases of care frame the couplet: parindhu ompi kaakka (‘guard it, cherishing it even through pain’) and therindhu ompi therinum (‘even after examining and weighing all’). The second line sounds almost empirical. After surveying the alternatives (wealth, learning, kin, other virtues), one finds that conduct is the only thunai, companion or support. Parimelazhagar and Pappaiah gloss thunai as the aid that goes with a person into this life and the next, which ties the couplet to a widespread image: good conduct is the one thing that ‘goes with’ a person at death. Karunanidhi stresses bearing hardship to keep it. Aristotle offers a close philosophical parallel when he calls virtuous activity more lasting than even scientific knowledge.

tamil:
ஒழுக்கம் உடைமை குடிமை இழுக்கம்
இழிந்த பிறப்பாய் விடும்.
transliteration:
Ozhukkam udaimai kudimai izhukkam
Izhindha pirappaai vidum.
current_meaning: Having right conduct is what makes a person nobly born. Falling away from it turns one's birth into a low one.
elementary_explanation: Coming from a ‘good family’ is not about your last name. If you act kindly and honestly, you are from a good family. If you behave badly, it is as if you did not come from a good family at all.
university_explanation: Kudimai (lineage, the dignity of one's house) is redefined here in terms of behaviour. Possessing ozhukkam is itself nobility of birth, while izhukkam (lapse, slipping) ‘becomes’ (aai vidum) a base birth. The verb matters: a lapse does not just disgrace one's family, it converts one's birth into a low one after the fact. Commentators differ on scope. Parimelazhagar and Pappaiah tie conduct to the duties of one's station, a view that fits a varna framework, while Varadarasanar and Karunanidhi read the couplet as a universal critique of status by birth. Either way, it belongs to a long Indian debate, also voiced by the Buddha in the Vasala Sutta and by Yudhishthira in the Mahabharata, over whether birth or behaviour makes a person noble.

tamil:
மறப்பினும் ஓத்துக் கொளலாகும் பார்ப்பான்
பிறப்பொழுக்கங் குன்றக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Marappinum oththuk kolalaagum paarppaan
Pirappozhukkam kundrak kedum.
current_meaning: A Brahmin who forgets the Vedas can learn them again. But if he falls away from the conduct that befits his birth, the birth itself is ruined.
elementary_explanation: If you forget your spelling words, you can study them again. But if you become a bully, no amount of studying fixes that. You lose something that is much harder to get back.
university_explanation: This couplet is the chapter's sharpest test case. The paarppaan (Brahmin) is the figure whose status depends most on birth and learning. Valluvar concedes that forgotten Vedic learning (oththu) can be recovered, but if pirappozhukkam, the conduct attached to that birth, declines (kundra), the birth itself is ruined (kedum). The logic is asymmetric: knowledge is a stock that can be replenished, while character is a foundation whose collapse brings down everything built on it. Commentators split between reading the couplet as upholding Brahmin duty (Parimelazhagar, Pappaiah) and as ranking birth below conduct (Karunanidhi). It closely echoes Manu 1.109, where a Brahmin who departs from the rule of conduct ‘does not reap the fruit of the Veda’, and Yudhishthira's answer to the Yaksha in the Mahabharata.

tamil:
அழுக்கா றுடையான்கண் ஆக்கம்போன்று இல்லை
ஒழுக்க மிலான்கண் உயர்வு.
transliteration:
Azhukkaaru udaiyaan-kan aakkampoandru illai
Ozhukkam ilaan-kan uyarvu.
current_meaning: Just as prosperity never settles on the envious, true eminence never comes to a person without right conduct.
elementary_explanation: A jealous kid spends so much time being upset about what others have that he never enjoys his own things. In the same way, someone who behaves badly never really rises high, no matter what.
university_explanation: The couplet works by analogy (ponru, ‘just as’). Azhukkaaru, envy, is so incompatible with aakkam (increase, prosperity) that its absence is proverbial, and uyarvu (elevation, rank) is just as surely absent from a person without ozhukkam. Envy gets a whole later chapter (17). Pappaiah reads uyarvu as ‘high lineage’, keeping the chapter's theme of birth, while Varadarasanar reads it as elevation in life generally. The pairing of envy with misconduct is deliberate: Tamil ethics treats envy as the model inner corruption that eats away at outward fortune, which a later couplet (Kural 168) develops. The claim is about incompatibility more than reward: certain dispositions cannot coexist with certain goods.

tamil:
ஒழுக்கத்தின் ஒல்கார் உரவோர் இழுக்கத்தின்
ஏதம் படுபாக் கறிந்து.
transliteration:
Ozhukkaththin olgaar uravoar izhukkaththin
Edham padupaak karindhu.
current_meaning: The strong-minded never slacken in their conduct, because they know the harm that follows a lapse.
elementary_explanation: A smart bike rider always wears a helmet, not because they are scared, but because they know how badly a fall can hurt. Strong people keep behaving well for the same reason: they know what happens when you don't.
university_explanation: Uravor, ‘the strong’, refers to strength of mind rather than of body (uram means firmness or resolve). Their steadiness is not naive. It rests on knowing (arindhu) the edham (fault, harm, calamity) that falls on those who lapse. That makes the couplet an argument about moral knowledge: firmness comes from seeing consequences clearly. Olkaar (‘they do not bend or slacken’) suggests constant, everyday vigilance rather than heroic resistance to one temptation. Pappaiah adds that they hold on ‘even when it is hard’ and reads the harm as loss of standing. Many traditions picture true strength as self-mastery: Ben Zoma's ‘Who is mighty?’, the Buddhist rock unshaken by the storm, and Odysseus binding himself because he knows what the Sirens do.

tamil:
ஒழுக்கத்தின் எய்துவர் மேன்மை இழுக்கத்தின்
எய்துவர் எய்தாப் பழி.
transliteration:
Ozhukkaththin eydhuvar menmai izhukkaththin
Eydhuvar eydhaap pazhi.
current_meaning: Through right conduct people rise to greatness. Through a lapse in it they earn a disgrace they never needed to suffer.
elementary_explanation: When you are kind and honest, people look up to you. When you cheat or lie, you get a bad name, and it is a bad name you could easily have avoided.
university_explanation: The couplet is built as a strict parallel: ozhukkaththin eydhuvar menmai / izhukkaththin eydhuvar eydhaap pazhi, ‘by conduct they attain eminence; by lapse they attain unattainable blame’. The paradoxical phrase eydhaap pazhi (‘blame that should not be attained’) is read in different ways: as undeserved, as unbearable, or as blame one had no need to incur. Pope's ‘censures undeserved’ takes the first reading, and most modern commentators take the last. Either way, the couplet makes the social stakes of conduct explicit, because menmai (eminence) and pazhi (blame) are verdicts passed by others. Here the chapter moves from inner firmness (136) to public consequence. The same pairing appears in Sanskrit dharmashastra, in the rabbinic ‘crown of a good name’, and in Hesiod's steep path to excellence.

tamil:
நன்றிக்கு வித்தாகும் நல்லொழுக்கம் தீயொழுக்கம்
என்றும் இடும்பை தரும்.
transliteration:
Nandrikku viththaagum nallozhukkam theeyozhukkam
Endrum idumbai tharum.
current_meaning: Good conduct is the seed from which good things grow. Bad conduct brings sorrow, always.
elementary_explanation: Plant an apple seed and you get an apple tree. Plant weeds and you get weeds. Being good is like planting a good seed, because nice things grow from it. Being mean only grows trouble.
university_explanation: The farming metaphor vittu (seed) makes nallozhukkam generative. Good conduct is not the good itself but the cause from which good (nandri, here ‘benefit’ or ‘virtue’ rather than ‘gratitude’, though one modern commentator reads it that way) grows over time. Its opposite, theeyozhukkam, gives idumbai (distress) endrum, ‘always’, which suggests a continuous harvest rather than a single punishment. Pappaiah extends the fruit to this life and the next (immai, marumai), which aligns the couplet with karmic causation, while Karunanidhi keeps it within this life. The seed image is nearly universal, from Paul's ‘whatsoever a man soweth’ to the Upanishadic ‘as he acts, so he becomes’ and Aristotle's view that character arises from like activities.

tamil:
ஒழுக்க முடையவர்க்கு ஒல்லாவே தீய
வழுக்கியும் வாயாற் சொலல்.
transliteration:
Ozhukkam udaiyavarkku ollaave theeya
Vazhukkiyum vaayaal solal.
current_meaning: People of right conduct cannot bring themselves to speak evil words, not even by a slip of the tongue.
elementary_explanation: Some people are so used to being kind that even when they are angry or surprised, mean words just don't come out. Being good becomes so natural that it even protects your mouth.
university_explanation: The key word is vazhukkiyum, ‘even when slipping’ or ‘even by inadvertence’. Valluvar does not say the disciplined hold back evil speech by effort. He says it is ollaa for them, impossible or unfitting: conduct has become so much second nature that even an unguarded moment is safe. This is a strong claim about habituation, close to Aristotle's view that the virtuous person does the right thing with pleasure and without inner struggle. Tamil ethics gives speech special attention, with chapters on sweet speech (10) and on avoiding useless speech (20). Parallel traditions do too: the Gita counts truthful, non-distressing speech as an austerity, rabbinic ethics condemns lashon hara, and Buddhism places right speech on the Eightfold Path.

tamil:
உலகத்தோடு ஒட்ட ஒழுகல் பலகற்றும்
கல்லார் அறிவிலா தார்.
transliteration:
Ulagaththoadu otta ozhugal pala-katrum
Kallaar arivilaa thaar.
current_meaning: People who have not learned to live in harmony with the world are ignorant, however many books they have studied.
elementary_explanation: Someone could read every book in the library, but if they cannot get along with people, share, or be polite, they have not really learned the most important lesson.
university_explanation: The chapter closes on a paradox: pala-katrum kallaar, ‘having learned much, they have not learned’. What they lack is ulagaththoadu otta ozhugal, conduct that ‘sticks to’ or fits with the world. Commentators differ on what ‘the world’ means. Parimelazhagar and Varadarasanar take it as the worthy (uyarndhor). Pappaiah boldly reads it as adapting the old ethical texts to present circumstances and dropping what no longer fits, which turns the couplet into almost a charter for moral reasoning over rote rule-following. On any reading, social wisdom is the test of learning. This echoes the rabbinic principle that derech eretz (right conduct) comes before Torah, and Aristotle's scorn for people who ‘take refuge in theory’.

tamil:
பிறன்பொருளாள் பெட்டொழுகும் பேதைமை ஞாலத்து
அறம்பொருள் கண்டார்கண் இல்.
transliteration:
Piranporulaal pettozhugum pedhaimai gnaalaththu,
Aramporul kandaarkan il.
current_meaning: The foolishness of desiring and pursuing a woman who belongs to another man is never found in those who have truly understood virtue and the right ordering of worldly life.
elementary_explanation: Imagine someone who has studied all the rules of a game very carefully. That person would never try to grab another player's pieces, because they understand how the game works and why the rules matter. This kural says people who really understand what is right and good would never want someone else's husband or wife.
university_explanation: Valluvar opens the chapter by framing adultery first as a failure of intelligence (பேதைமை, 'folly') rather than simply as a sin. The phrase அறம்பொருள் கண்டார் — 'those who have seen aram and porul' — deliberately invokes the first two aims of life that structure the Kural itself (virtue and worldly prosperity), implying that a person who grasps either domain properly would recognise such desire as self-defeating. The word பொருளாள் ('she who is another's porul') reflects the social vocabulary of its age, in which a wife was spoken of as belonging within another's household; modern readers often recast it as a violation of another's committed bond. The kural thus locates the root of the wrong in ignorance, a move that parallels Socratic and Buddhist views that wrongdoing flows from failed understanding.

tamil:
அறன்கடை நின்றாருள் எல்லாம் பிறன்கடை
நின்றாரின் பேதையார் இல்.
transliteration:
Arankadai nindraarul ellaam pirankadai,
Nindraarin pedhaiyaar il.
current_meaning: Of all the people who stand outside the bounds of virtue, none is more foolish than the one who lingers at another man's door, longing for his wife.
elementary_explanation: Think of all the silly, wrong things people can do. This kural says that out of all of them, the silliest is waiting outside a neighbour's house because you want the person who belongs to that family. It is the worst kind of wrong choice.
university_explanation: The couplet turns on a pun with the word கடை, which can mean both 'the outermost/lowest point' and 'a gate or doorway': அறன்கடை ('beyond the edge of virtue') is set against பிறன்கடை ('at another's gate'). Valluvar thus ranks wrongdoers and places the would-be adulterer, loitering at a neighbour's door, at the very bottom for sheer foolishness. The image of standing at the gate stresses both the humiliation of the act and its risk: the man is exposed, waiting, and dependent on another's household. Commentators such as Parimelazhagar read this as a claim that even among sinners this particular vice is uniquely irrational, because it brings danger without any lasting gain.

tamil:
விளிந்தாரின் வேறல்லர் மன்ற தெளிந்தாரில்
தீமை புரிந்துதொழுகு வார்.
transliteration:
Vilindhaarin verallar mandra thelindhaaril,
Theemai purindhozhugu vaar.
current_meaning: Those who plot wrong against the household of people who trust them without doubt are surely no different from the dead.
elementary_explanation: Suppose a friend trusts you so much that they let you into their home anytime. If you used that trust to try to take what is most precious to their family, you would be like a broken, empty person inside, with nothing good left alive in you. That is what this kural says.
university_explanation: The key word தெளிந்தார் means 'those who are clear' or 'those who trust without suspicion': the victims here are friends who have let the man into their home precisely because they do not doubt him. Valluvar's verdict, விளிந்தாரின் வேறல்லர் ('not different from the dead'), is a moral rather than literal death: the betrayer has extinguished what makes a person trustworthy and therefore socially alive. Commentators note the intensifier மன்ற ('certainly'), which removes any softening. The couplet thus adds betrayal of trust to the chapter's charge of folly, anticipating the ancient idea, shared by Stoics and scriptural traditions, that faithlessness destroys the essence of a human being.

tamil:
எனைத்துணையர் ஆயினும் என்னாம் தினைத்துணையும்
தேரான் பிறனில் புகல்.
transliteration:
Enaiththunaiyar aayinum ennaam thinaiththunaiyum,
Theraan piranil pugal.
current_meaning: However great a man may be, what is his greatness worth if he enters another man's home for his wife without weighing his wrong even a little?
elementary_explanation: Imagine the best player on a team, who is famous and loved by everyone. If that player cheated in a very unfair way without stopping to think, all their fame would be worth nothing. This kural says the same about a person who goes after someone else's husband or wife: being important cannot save them.
university_explanation: The couplet plays two measures against each other: எனைத்துணை ('however great a measure') and தினைத்துணை ('a millet grain's measure'), the smallest unit in Tamil idiom. A man may possess vast greatness, yet if he does not reflect (தேரான்) for even a millet grain's worth before entering another's home, that greatness is worthless. The rhetorical question என்னாம் ('what does it become?') leaves the answer, nothing, to the listener. The emphasis on failing to reflect links to the chapter's theme of folly: the danger lies in the thoughtless moment in which rank and reputation are thrown away, a pattern visible in stories of kings and heroes across many cultures.

tamil:
எளிதென இல்லிறப்பான் எய்துமெஞ் ஞான்றும்
விளியாது நிற்கும் பழி.
transliteration:
Elidhena illirappaan eydhum enjnjaandrum,
Viliyaadhu nirkum pazhi.
current_meaning: The man who crosses into another's household, thinking it an easy thing, earns a disgrace that never dies and stays with him forever.
elementary_explanation: Some mistakes are like writing on sand: they wash away. Others are like carving into stone: they stay forever. This kural says that going after someone else's husband or wife might seem easy at the time, but the shame is carved in stone and never goes away.
university_explanation: Valluvar contrasts the ease of the act (எளிது, 'easy') with the permanence of its consequence (விளியாது நிற்கும் பழி, 'blame that stands undying'). The verb இல்லிறப்பான் combines இல் ('home') and இறப்பு ('crossing over, transgressing'), so the offender is literally 'one who oversteps a home'. The couplet reflects a culture where reputation (புகழ்) was treated as the only thing that outlives a person, a theme developed in the Kural's later chapter on fame; adultery produces the exact opposite, a lasting infamy. The asymmetry between a moment's ease and an eternity of blame is a common moral argument, found in scriptural warnings about reproach that 'shall not be wiped away'.

tamil:
பகைபாவம் அச்சம் பழியென நான்கும்
இகவாவாம் இல்லிறப்பான் கண்.
transliteration:
Pagaipaavam achcham pazhiyena naangum,
Igavaavaam illirappaan kan.
current_meaning: Enmity, sin, fear, and disgrace: these four never leave the man who transgresses against another's home.
elementary_explanation: Picture someone who takes a thing that belongs to another family. Now four shadows follow them everywhere: people are angry at them, they know they did wrong, they are always scared of being caught, and others think badly of them. This kural says those four shadows never go away.
university_explanation: This couplet is a compact catalogue: பகை (enmity from the wronged husband and his kin), பாவம் (sin, the moral or karmic stain), அச்சம் (constant fear of discovery and revenge), and பழி (public blame). The verb இகவா ('they do not depart') makes all four permanent companions. The list covers the social, spiritual, psychological, and reputational costs of the act, a strikingly complete analysis for two lines. Its closest parallel is Dhammapada 309, which also names exactly four misfortunes for the man who goes to another's wife, a resemblance that scholars have noted when discussing shared ethical currents in early South Asian literature.

tamil:
அறனியலான் இல்வாழ்வான் என்பான் பிறனியலாள்
பெண்மை நயவா தவன்.
transliteration:
Araniyalaan ilvaazhvaan enbaan piraniyalaal,
Penmai nayavaa thavan.
current_meaning: The one who is called a true householder, living by the way of virtue, is the man who does not desire the womanhood of one who belongs to another.
elementary_explanation: What makes someone a good member of a family? This kural gives a simple test: a good family person is happy with their own family and never wishes for someone else's husband or wife. Being loyal is part of being good at home.
university_explanation: Here Valluvar turns from warning to definition: the true இல்வாழ்வான் (householder), the central figure of the whole இல்லறவியல் section, is identified by a negative mark, not desiring பிறனியலாள் ('she who moves within another's sphere'). The word இயல் appears twice, linking அறன்இயலான் ('one whose conduct is shaped by virtue') to பிறன்இயலாள் ('one whose life is joined to another'), so the couplet balances two kinds of belonging. By defining domestic virtue through fidelity, the Kural treats chastity as a duty of husbands as much as of wives, which some modern commentators highlight as notably even-handed for its era. The idea that the good household is built on the spouse's exclusive devotion appears in many traditions' ideals of marriage.

tamil:
பிறன்மனை நோக்காத பேராண்மை சான்றோர்க்கு
அறனொன்றோ ஆன்ற வொழுக்கு.
transliteration:
Piranmanai nokkaadha peraanmai saandrorkku,
Aranondro aandra ozhukku.
current_meaning: The great manliness that does not even look with desire at another's wife is, for the noble, not merely virtue but the fullness of right conduct.
elementary_explanation: Being truly strong is not about big muscles. This kural says real strength is choosing not even to look at someone else's husband or wife in a wanting way. That kind of self-control is the strongest and best way to behave.
university_explanation: The striking term பேராண்மை ('great manliness' or 'supreme valour') redefines heroism: in a culture that prized martial courage, Valluvar says the greatest valour is the self-mastery not to look (நோக்காத) at another's wife with desire. The couplet moves the moral line from the act to the gaze, the same shift found in the Sermon on the Mount and in the Qur'anic command to lower the gaze. The second line says this restraint is not just one virtue (அறன் ஒன்றோ, 'is it only virtue?') but ஆன்ற ஒழுக்கு, complete or mature conduct, linking this chapter back to the preceding chapter on ஒழுக்கமுடைமை (right conduct). For the சான்றோர் (the noble or accomplished), then, this restraint is the crown of character.

tamil:
நலக்குரியார் யாரெனின் நாமநீர் வைப்பின்
பிறர்க்குரியாள் தோள்தோயா தார்.
transliteration:
Nalakkuriyaar yaarenin naamaneer vaippin,
Pirarkkuriyaal tholthoyaa thaar.
current_meaning: If you ask who, in this world surrounded by the fearsome sea, truly deserves every good thing, it is those who do not embrace a woman who belongs to another.
elementary_explanation: If you asked, 'Who deserves all the best things in the whole wide world?', this kural has an answer: the people who stay loyal and never go after someone else's husband or wife. Being faithful makes you worthy of good things.
university_explanation: The couplet is framed as a question and answer, a device Valluvar uses to give his verdict extra force. The phrase நாமநீர் வைப்பு ('the world set within fearsome waters') is a classical Tamil epithet for the earth encircled by the ocean, so the claim is universal: anywhere in the world. The one worthy of நலம் (goodness, blessing, well-being) is identified by a concrete image, தோள் தோயாதார் ('those whose shoulders do not touch'), an embrace withheld. After several couplets on the ruin that follows adultery, this one reverses the angle and promises reward, showing that the chapter aims to encourage as well as warn.

tamil:
அறன்வரையான் அல்ல செயினும் பிறன்வரையாள்
பெண்மை நயவாமை நன்று.
transliteration:
Aranvaraiyaan alla seyinum piranvaraiyaal,
Penmai nayavaamai nandru.
current_meaning: Even if a man lives outside the bounds of virtue and does many wrong things, it is still good that he at least not desire the womanhood of one who lives within another's bounds.
elementary_explanation: Imagine someone who breaks lots of rules. This kural says: even if they have not been good at many things, they should at least keep this one rule and never go after someone else's husband or wife. It is the one line everyone must never cross.
university_explanation: The closing couplet makes a realistic concession: even a man who does not stay within virtue's limits (அறன் வரையான்) and does what should not be done (அல்ல செயினும்) should at least not desire one who lives within another's limits (பிறன் வரையாள்). The repetition of வரை ('boundary') creates a pointed wordplay: he may cross the bounds of virtue, but must not cross the bounds of another's marriage. By holding this line even for the imperfect, Valluvar marks adultery as a floor below which no one should fall, not merely an ideal for saints. The move is pastoral as well as moral, offering even the flawed a place to begin.
